# Karma

## Canonical Name

Karma

## Sanskrit

कर्म

## Transliteration

Karma

## Śabda

कर्म

## Dhātu

कृ (Kṛ) — To do, perform, act, make.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from the verbal root कृ (kṛ) with the suffix -man (neuter noun). Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.3.18. Karma is a neuter noun meaning "action" or "deed." In grammar, karma also denotes the object of a verb (karman = object/patient).

## Nirukta

Yāska: "kriyate anena iti karma" — that by which action is performed. The root kṛ encompasses all forms of doing, making, and performing.

## Bīja

क (Ka) — the seed syllable of action and creation in Tantric traditions. Associated with Brahmā (the creator) whose bīja is also Ka.

## Tattva

Karma-Tattva — the principle of causation through action. In Sāṃkhya: karma is the activity of the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas). In Vaiśeṣika: karma is one of the seven padārthas (categories), defined as motion. In Vedānta: karma is the mechanism of saṃsāra (cycle of rebirth).

## Śakti

Kriyā-Śakti — the power of action. One of the three fundamental śaktis (icchā-jñāna-kriyā). Karma operates through kriyā-śakti as the dynamic force of manifestation.

## Literal Meaning

Action; deed; work; ritual act.

## Functional Meaning

Karma is the universal principle that every action generates corresponding consequences. It operates across three dimensions: Sañcita karma (accumulated past actions), Prārabdha karma (karma currently bearing fruit), and Āgāmi/Kriyamāṇa karma (karma being created now). The law of karma is not punishment but the natural law of cause and effect operating through consciousness.

## Ontology

In Mīmāṃsā: karma (ritual action) is the primary means of achieving dharmic results; the apūrva (unseen potency) of ritual karma persists until it bears fruit. In Advaita Vedānta: karma operates only at the vyāvahārika level; from the absolute standpoint, there is no doer, hence no karma. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: karma is real and must be exhausted through bhakti and surrender to Viṣṇu. In Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika: karma is one of seven categories of reality, defined as motion (pariṇāma).

## Cosmology

Karma drives the cycle of saṃsāra across all fourteen lokas. The Purāṇas describe karma as the mechanism by which souls transmigrate through different realms. In Jain cosmology, karma is a subtle material substance (karma-pudgala) that adheres to the soul (jīva) and determines its condition. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa describes karma as the force that maintains the cosmic order of creation, preservation, and dissolution.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology: karma creates saṃskāras (mental impressions) and vāsanās (latent tendencies) that condition future experience. Patañjali's Yoga Sūtras 2.12-14 describe the karma-āśaya (karma-store) as the root of birth, lifespan, and experience. Karma operates through the kāraṇa-śarīra (causal body). Karma yoga (the yoga of action) transforms karma from bondage to liberation by eliminating the sense of doership (ahaṃkāra).

## Marathi Summary

कर्मयोग म्हणजे आपले कर्तव्यकर्म करणे, पण त्याच्या फळाची आसक्ती न ठेवणे. अशा कृतीतून अहंभाव कमी होतो आणि कर्मबंधनातून मुक्त होण्याचा मार्ग मिळतो.

## Governance

Karma as social principle: the concept of karma-phala (fruit of action) underlies Indian jurisprudence. Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra recognizes that rulers accumulate karma through their governance. The concept of rāja-dharma (royal duty) is the karmic responsibility of the king. Historical Indian governance was explicitly framed in karmic terms — Aśoka's dhamma edicts reflect karmic accountability.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: karma is one of the causes of disease (prājñāparādha — crime against wisdom is a karmic cause). Caraka Saṃhitā identifies karma as a factor in the etiology of disease. Karmic diseases (ādhidaivika) require spiritual remedies alongside physical treatment. The concept of karma-ja-vyādhi (karma-born disease) is a distinct category in Āyurvedic pathology.

## Mathematics

The mathematical principle of karma is the law of conservation: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Vedic mathematics (Gaṇita) treats karma as the principle of balance — equations must balance, debts must be settled. The concept of ṛṇa (debt) in Vedic mathematics mirrors the karmic debt concept.

## Astronomy

Karma in Jyotiṣa (Vedic astrology): the birth chart (janma-kuṇḍali) is considered a map of prārabdha karma. Planetary positions at birth reflect accumulated karma. The concept of daśā (planetary period) describes the timing of karmic fruition. Graha (planets) are considered agents of karma delivery.

## Metallurgy

In Viśvakarmā tradition: the karma of the craftsman (śilpin) determines the quality of the work. The concept of karma-yoga in craft: the craftsman who works without attachment to results produces the finest work. The dharma of metals (their inherent properties) must be respected — working against a metal's karma produces inferior results.

## Ritual

Karma-kāṇḍa (ritual section of the Vedas) is the primary domain of Mīmāṃsā. The sixteen saṃskāras are karmic rituals that shape the individual's karmic trajectory. Yajña (sacrifice) is the highest karmic act — it purifies accumulated karma and generates positive karma. Prāyaścitta (expiation) rituals neutralize specific karmic debts.

## Symbolism

The wheel (cakra) symbolizes karma's cyclical nature. The scales represent karmic balance. The seed (bīja) represents karma's potential — every action is a seed that will bear fruit. The mirror represents karma's reflective nature — what you do returns to you. The knot (granthi) represents karmic bondage.

## Related Deities

- Yama (Dharmarāja — lord of karmic accounting and death)
- Citragupta (Yama's scribe who records all karma)
- Śani (Saturn — the planet of karmic lessons and consequences)
- Brahmā (the creator who sets karma in motion)
- Viṣṇu (the preserver who maintains karmic order)

## Related Lokas

- Naraka (hell realms — destination of negative karma)
- Svarga (heaven realms — destination of positive karma)
- Pitṛloka (realm of ancestors — intermediate karmic state)
- Bhūloka (earth — the primary field of karmic action)

## Related Koshas

- Kāraṇa Śarīra (causal body) — the storehouse of accumulated karma (sañcita karma)
- Sūkṣma Śarīra (subtle body) — the vehicle through which karma is experienced
- Manomaya Kosha (mind sheath) — where karmic intentions originate

## Related Chakras

- Maṇipūra (solar plexus chakra) — seat of will, action, and karmic agency
- Mūlādhāra (root chakra) — seat of prārabdha karma and survival instincts
- Svādhiṣṭhāna (sacral chakra) — seat of karmic desires and creative action

## Related Yantras

- Karma Yantra (used in rituals for karmic purification)
- Śani Yantra (for mitigating difficult karmic periods)

## Related Mantras

- "Karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.47) — You have the right to action alone, never to its fruits
- Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra (for liberation from karmic death-cycle)
- Śani Mantra: "Om śam śanaiścarāya namaḥ" (for karmic lessons)

## Related Vidyās

- Karma-Yoga Vidyā (science of action without attachment)
- Jyotiṣa Vidyā (science of karmic timing)
- Prāyaścitta Vidyā (science of karmic expiation)

## Related Śāstras

- Bhagavad Gītā (Chapters 3, 4, 5 — Karma Yoga)
- Mīmāṃsā Sūtras (Jaimini) — ritual karma
- Yoga Sūtras (Patañjali) 2.12-14 — karma-āśaya
- Tattvartha Sūtra (Umāsvāti) — Jain karma doctrine
- Caraka Saṃhitā — karmic disease

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Karma is ultimately unreal from the absolute standpoint; jñāna (knowledge) alone destroys karma
- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Karma is real and must be surrendered to Viṣṇu through prapatti (surrender)
- Dvaita (Madhva): Karma is eternally real; liberation requires Viṣṇu's grace to transcend karma
- Mīmāṃsā: Karma (ritual action) is the primary means of achieving all human goals
- Buddhism: Karma is intentional action (cetanā); it is the intention, not the act, that creates karma
- Jainism: Karma is a subtle material substance that binds the soul; liberation requires exhausting all karma through tapas (austerity)

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Karma primarily means ritual action; cosmic karma (ṛta) governs the universe
- Brāhmaṇa period: Karma as ritual action is elaborated extensively; karma-kāṇḍa develops
- Upaniṣadic period: Karma as ethical-spiritual principle emerges; karma-saṃsāra connection established
- Buddhist period (500 BCE): Karma redefined as intentional action; karma-rebirth doctrine systematized
- Jain period: Karma as material substance — unique and influential formulation
- Epic-Purāṇic period: Karma as cosmic justice mechanism; karma-yoga as path to liberation
- Medieval: Karma integrated into bhakti traditions — karma surrendered to God

## Cross References

- Dharma
- Moksha
- Yoga
- Saṃskāra
- Punarjanma (rebirth)
- Ahaṃkāra (ego — the false doer)
- Vāsanā (latent tendencies)

## Open Research Questions

- Is karma a deterministic or probabilistic system? Can free will operate within karma?
- What is the relationship between Vedic karma (ritual action) and Buddhist karma (intentional action)?
- How does the Jain material karma theory relate to the Vedic subtle-body karma theory?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some researchers propose that karma theory anticipates modern concepts of information conservation in physics — that the "information" of every action is preserved in the universe. This remains speculative and is not established in any canonical tradition.

## Canonical Sources

- Bhagavad Gītā 2.47, 3.5, 4.17
- Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13 (karma-rebirth connection)
- Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10 (karma and rebirth)
- Yoga Sūtras 2.12-14
- Tattvartha Sūtra (Umāsvāti) — Jain karma
- Mīmāṃsā Sūtras (Jaimini)

# Dharma

## Canonical Name

Dharma

## Sanskrit

धर्म

## Transliteration

Dharma

## Śabda

धर्म

## Dhātu

धृ (Dhṛ) — To uphold, sustain, support.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from the verbal root धृ (dhṛ) with the suffix -man. Masculine noun, second declension. Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.3.18 governs the suffix formation.

## Nirukta

Yāska's Nirukta: "dharayati iti dharmaḥ" — that which upholds is Dharma. The root dhṛ carries the sense of bearing, sustaining, maintaining cosmic and social order.

## Bīja

ध (Dha) — the seed syllable associated with sustaining force in Tantric traditions.

## Tattva

Ṛta-Dharma Tattva — the principle of cosmic and moral order that sustains all existence. In Sāṃkhya: Dharma is a quality (guṇa) of the Mahat (cosmic intellect). In Vedānta: Dharma is the expression of Ṛta at the human level.

## Śakti

Dharma-Śakti — the preserving and ordering power. Associated with Viṣṇu's sustaining function (sthiti-śakti). In Śākta traditions, Dharma is upheld by the Goddess as Mahāmāyā maintaining cosmic law.

## Literal Meaning

That which is upheld; that which upholds. The sustaining principle.

## Functional Meaning

Dharma is the universal principle governing righteous conduct, cosmic order, social duty, and individual ethics. It operates simultaneously at four levels: Ṛta (cosmic order), Varṇāśrama-dharma (social order), Svadharma (individual duty), and Sādhāraṇa-dharma (universal ethics applicable to all beings).

## Marathi Summary

धर्म म्हणजे योग्य आचरण, सामाजिक कर्तव्य, वैश्विक व्यवस्था आणि सर्वांसाठी लागू होणारी नैतिकता टिकवून ठेवणारे तत्त्व.

## Ontology

In Vaiśeṣika: Dharma is a padārtha (category of reality) — the cause of abhyudaya (worldly prosperity) and niḥśreyasa (liberation). In Mīmāṃsā: Dharma is codanā-lakṣaṇa — that which is enjoined by Vedic injunction. In Advaita Vedānta: Dharma at the vyāvahārika (conventional) level is real and necessary; at the pāramārthika (absolute) level, only Brahman exists.

## Cosmology

Dharma is one of the four Puruṣārthas (aims of human life): Dharma, Artha, Kāma, Mokṣa. In the Purāṇic cosmology, Dharma is personified as a deity, son of Brahmā, husband of ten daughters of Dakṣa. In the four yugas (Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali), Dharma stands on four legs, three, two, and one respectively — indicating progressive decline of cosmic order.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology (Patañjali): Dharma-megha-samādhi is the highest samādhi, the "cloud of virtue" that rains liberation. Dharma as psychological principle governs the sattva-rajas-tamas balance in the individual. Right action (dharmic action) produces psychological clarity (citta-prasāda).

## Governance

Rājadharma (royal duty) is elaborated in Manusmṛti, Arthaśāstra, Mahābhārata Śāntiparva. The king's primary duty is dharma-rakṣaṇa (protection of dharma). Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra treats dharma as the foundation of statecraft. Aśoka's dhamma edicts represent the historical application of dharmic governance.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Dharma is the foundation of Āyurvedic ethics. The physician's svadharma includes ahiṃsā (non-harm), satya (truth), and service. Caraka Saṃhitā Sūtrasthāna 1.15 states that the physician who follows dharma achieves both worldly success and liberation.

## Mathematics

Dharma as cosmic order underlies the mathematical precision of Vedic ritual geometry (Śulbasūtras). The Pythagorean theorem appears in Baudhāyana Śulbasūtra as a dharmic requirement for altar construction. Mathematical truth (satya) is considered a form of dharma.

## Astronomy

Ṛta (cosmic order, precursor to dharma) governs the movements of celestial bodies. Vedic astronomy (Jyotiṣa) treats planetary motion as dharmic — planets follow their ordained paths. The concept of ṛtu (season) derives from ṛta, linking dharma to astronomical cycles.

## Metallurgy

In Viśvakarmā tradition: the dharma of metals is their inherent nature and proper use. Gold (suvarṇa) has the dharma of purity; iron (ayasa) has the dharma of strength. Proper metallurgical practice follows the dharma of each material.

## Ritual

Yajña (sacrifice) is the primary ritual expression of dharma. The Mīmāṃsā school holds that Vedic ritual injunctions (vidhi) define dharma. Dharma-śāstra prescribes the sixteen saṃskāras (life-cycle rituals) as the ritual framework of dharmic life. Sandhyāvandana (daily worship) is the minimal dharmic ritual obligation.

## Symbolism

Dharma is symbolized by the wheel (dharmacakra) — the Buddha's first teaching is the "turning of the wheel of dharma." The scales of justice represent dharma's balancing function. The lotus represents dharma's purity amid worldly existence. The cow (go) is the living symbol of dharma in Vedic tradition.

## Related Deities

- Viṣṇu (Dharma's primary upholder; avatāras descend to restore dharma)
- Yama (Dharmarāja — lord of dharma and death)
- Mitra (Vedic deity of contracts and dharmic agreements)
- Varuṇa (upholder of ṛta, cosmic dharma)
- Indra (protector of dharmic order against adharma)

## Related Lokas

- Dharmaloka (realm of righteous souls)
- Satyaloka (Brahmaloka — realm of ultimate dharma)
- Pitṛloka (realm governed by ancestral dharma)

## Related Koshas

- Vijñānamaya Kosha (intellect sheath) — the seat of dharmic discrimination (viveka)
- Manomaya Kosha (mind sheath) — where dharmic intentions form
- Ānandamaya Kosha (bliss sheath) — the state of perfect dharmic alignment

## Related Chakras

- Anāhata (heart chakra) — seat of dharmic compassion and right relationship
- Ājñā (third eye chakra) — seat of dharmic wisdom and discrimination
- Sahasrāra (crown chakra) — union with cosmic dharma (Ṛta)

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (represents the cosmic order that dharma upholds)
- Dharma Yantra (specific to dharmic protection rituals)

## Related Mantras

- "Dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ" (Manusmṛti 8.15) — Dharma protects those who protect it
- Gāyatrī Mantra (the foundational mantra of dharmic life)
- "Satyam vada, dharmam cara" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.1) — Speak truth, follow dharma

## Related Vidyās

- Dharmaśāstra Vidyā (science of righteous law)
- Rājadharma Vidyā (science of governance)
- Ātmavidyā (self-knowledge as the highest dharma)

## Related Śāstras

- Manusmṛti (primary dharmaśāstra)
- Yājñavalkya Smṛti
- Arthaśāstra (Kauṭilya)
- Mahābhārata (Śāntiparva, Anuśāsanaparva)
- Dharmasūtras of Āpastamba, Gautama, Baudhāyana

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Dharma is ultimately subsumed in jñāna (knowledge); it is a means, not the end
- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Dharma is bhakti-yoga — devotional service to Viṣṇu is the highest dharma
- Dvaita (Madhva): Dharma is the eternal will of Viṣṇu; individual dharma is participation in divine order
- Mīmāṃsā (Jaimini): Dharma is exclusively Vedic injunction; no dharma exists outside Veda
- Buddhism: Dharma is the teaching of the Buddha and the nature of reality (dhamma)
- Jainism: Dharma is the medium of motion (one of the six dravyas); also righteous conduct (dharma)

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Ṛta (cosmic order) is the precursor; dharma appears rarely
- Atharvaveda: Dharma begins to acquire social and ethical dimensions
- Upaniṣadic period: Dharma becomes internalized as ethical-spiritual principle
- Epic period (Mahābhārata): Dharma becomes the central problematic — the Gītā's entire teaching is dharmic
- Dharmaśāstra period (200 BCE–1200 CE): Systematic codification of dharma in law texts
- Colonial period: Dharma reinterpreted through encounter with Western legal concepts
- Modern: Dharma as "religion" (mistranslation) vs. dharma as cosmic-ethical principle (ongoing debate)

## Cross References

- Karma
- Moksha
- Yoga
- Ṛta
- Artha
- Kāma
- Ahiṃsā
- Satya
- Yajña

## Open Research Questions

- What is the precise relationship between Ṛta (Vedic cosmic order) and Dharma (post-Vedic ethical order)?
- How did dharma evolve from a purely ritual concept (Mīmāṃsā) to a universal ethical principle?
- Can dharma function as a cross-cultural ethical framework in contemporary governance?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some scholars hypothesize that the Vedic concept of Ṛta influenced early Iranian Asha (truth/order) and possibly Greek Themis (divine law). This cross-cultural connection remains under scholarly investigation and is not established canon.

## Canonical Sources

- Ṛgveda (Ṛta passages: 1.22.18, 1.105.12, 4.23.8)
- Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.1
- Bhagavad Gītā (Chapter 4: Jñāna-Karma-Sannyāsa Yoga)
- Manusmṛti
- Mahābhārata (Śāntiparva)
- Arthaśāstra (Kauṭilya)
- Dharmasūtras (Āpastamba, Gautama)

# Guru

## Canonical Name

Guru

## Sanskrit

गुरु

## Transliteration

Guru

## Śabda

गुरु

## Dhātu

गृ (Gṛ) — To swallow, to take in; also connected to गुर् (Gur) — heavy, weighty. The guru is the "heavy one" — weighty with knowledge.

## Vyākaraṇa

Guru is an adjective (meaning "heavy, weighty, important") used as a noun. It is also used as a title. The feminine form is Gurū or Gurviṇī. The word is used in both the sense of "teacher" and "heavy/important."

## Nirukta

"Gu-kāraś cāndhakārasya ru-kāras tannirodhakṛt" — Gu represents darkness (ignorance), Ru represents its removal. The Guru is one who removes the darkness of ignorance. This etymology appears in the Advayatāraka Upaniṣad.

## Bīja

गुं (Guṃ) — the bīja associated with the Guru principle in Tantric traditions.

## Tattva

Guru-Tattva — the principle of the teacher who transmits knowledge and removes ignorance. In Kashmir Śaivism: Guru-tattva is one of the thirty-six tattvas — the principle of divine grace operating through the human teacher.

## Śakti

Guru-Śakti — the power of the teacher to transmit knowledge and grace. The concept of śakti-pāta (descent of grace) — the Guru's transmission of spiritual power to the student.

## Literal Meaning

Heavy; weighty; important; teacher; spiritual master.

## Functional Meaning

The Guru is the teacher who transmits knowledge (vidyā) from the tradition to the student. In the Vedic tradition, knowledge cannot be obtained from books alone — it must be transmitted from Guru to student in an unbroken lineage (paramparā). The Guru removes the student's ignorance (avidyā) and guides them toward liberation (mokṣa). The Guru-śiṣya (teacher-student) relationship is the foundational relationship of Indian civilization.

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta: the Guru is the external manifestation of the inner Guru (Ātman). The Guru's teaching points the student to their own true nature. In Tantra: the Guru is the living embodiment of the divine — "Guru is Brahma, Guru is Viṣṇu, Guru is Maheśvara" (Guru Gītā). In Kashmir Śaivism: the Guru is the agent of Śiva's grace — śakti-pāta operates through the Guru.

## Cosmology

In Purāṇic cosmology: Bṛhaspati is the Guru of the gods (deva-guru); Śukra is the Guru of the demons (asura-guru). The concept of Ādi-Guru (the first Guru) — Śiva is the Ādi-Guru who taught yoga to Pārvatī. The concept of Guru-paramparā (lineage of teachers) — the unbroken chain from the divine source to the present teacher.

## Psychology

The Guru-śiṣya relationship as psychological transformation: the Guru mirrors the student's unconscious patterns and guides their dissolution. The concept of guru-bhakti (devotion to the Guru) as a psychological practice — surrendering the ego to the Guru's guidance. The concept of guru-kṛpā (Guru's grace) — the transformative power of the Guru's attention and blessing.

## Governance

The concept of Guru in governance: the rāja-guru (royal teacher) was the king's spiritual and political advisor. Cāṇakya (Kauṭilya) was the paradigmatic rāja-guru — he guided Candragupta Maurya to establish the Maurya Empire. The concept of dharma-guru (teacher of righteousness) — the Guru who guides the ruler in dharmic governance.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: the Guru is the teacher of medical knowledge. The Guru-śiṣya relationship is the primary mode of Āyurvedic transmission. The concept of guru-upadeśa (Guru's instruction) as the most important element of Āyurvedic education. The Guru's direct observation and correction of the student's practice is essential.

## Mathematics

The concept of Guru in mathematics: the transmission of mathematical knowledge through the Guru-śiṣya relationship. The Āryabhaṭīya and other mathematical texts were transmitted through Guru-paramparā. The concept of guru-mukha-vidyā (knowledge from the Guru's mouth) — mathematical knowledge that cannot be obtained from texts alone.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Guru (Jupiter) is the planet of wisdom, teaching, and expansion. Jupiter is the Guru of the solar system — the largest planet, the teacher of the other planets. The concept of guru-bala (Jupiter's strength) in the birth chart — a strong Jupiter indicates wisdom and good teachers.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: the Guru is the master alchemist who transmits the secret knowledge of Rasaśāstra. The concept of guru-dīkṣā (initiation by the Guru) in alchemy — the student cannot practice alchemy without the Guru's initiation and guidance.

## Ritual

The Guru-pūjā (worship of the Guru) is performed on Guru Pūrṇimā (the full moon of Āṣāḍha). The Guru-vandanā (salutation to the Guru) begins all learning. The concept of guru-dakṣiṇā (gift to the Guru) — the student's offering to the Guru upon completion of study. The Upanayana saṃskāra initiates the student into the Guru-śiṣya relationship.

## Symbolism

The lamp (dīpa) symbolizes the Guru — the Guru's knowledge illuminates the student's darkness. The sun symbolizes the Guru — the source of light and life. The river symbolizes the Guru's teaching — it flows from the source (tradition) to nourish the student.

## Related Deities

- Bṛhaspati (the Guru of the gods — the divine teacher)
- Dattātreya (the Guru of all gurus — the avadhūta teacher)
- Śiva (Ādi-Guru — the first teacher of yoga)
- Sarasvatī (the Goddess of learning — the divine Guru)
- Gaṇeśa (the remover of obstacles in learning)

## Related Lokas

- Guru-loka (the realm of the teacher — Jupiter's realm)
- Brahmaloka (the destination of the student who follows the Guru's teaching)

## Related Koshas

- Vijñānamaya Kosha (intellect sheath) — the primary domain of the Guru's teaching
- Ānandamaya Kosha (bliss sheath) — the domain of the Guru's grace

## Related Chakras

- Ājñā (third eye chakra) — the seat of the inner Guru
- Sahasrāra (crown chakra) — the seat of the Guru's grace (guru-pīṭha)

## Related Yantras

- Guru Yantra (for invoking the Guru's grace)
- Bṛhaspati Yantra (for Jupiter's wisdom)

## Related Mantras

- "Gurur Brahmā gurur Viṣṇuḥ gurur devo Maheśvaraḥ, Guru sākṣāt paraṃ Brahma tasmai śrī gurave namaḥ" (Guru Gītā)
- Guru Gāyatrī: "Om gurudevāya vidmahe parambrahmāya dhīmahi"

## Related Vidyās

- Guru-Vidyā (the science of the teacher-student relationship)
- Guru-Gītā (the teaching of the Guru — from the Skanda Purāṇa)

## Related Śāstras

- Guru Gītā (Skanda Purāṇa — the primary text on the Guru)
- Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11 (the Guru's final instructions to the student)
- Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12 (the necessity of the Guru)
- Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.8 (the Guru who knows Brahman)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita: The Guru is the external manifestation of the inner Guru (Ātman)
- Tantra: The Guru is the living embodiment of the divine — Guru = Brahman
- Vaiṣṇava: The Guru is the representative of Viṣṇu — serving the Guru is serving God
- Kashmir Śaivism: The Guru is the agent of Śiva's grace

## Historical Evolution

- Vedic period: The Guru as the teacher of the Vedas in the gurukula
- Upaniṣadic period: The Guru as the transmitter of Brahmavidyā
- Classical period: The Guru-śiṣya relationship systematized
- Tantric period: The Guru as the initiator and transmitter of śakti
- Modern: The Guru concept challenged and reinterpreted

## Cross References

- Vidya
- Samskara (Upanayana — the saṃskāra of entering the Guru's household)
- Dharma
- Brahman

## Open Research Questions

- What is the epistemological basis of the claim that certain knowledge can only be transmitted from Guru to student, not from texts?
- How does the Guru-śiṣya relationship function in the modern context where traditional gurukulas no longer exist?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some researchers propose that the Guru-śiṣya relationship functions as a form of mentored neuroplasticity — the Guru's guidance shapes the student's neural patterns in ways that self-study cannot. This remains under investigation.

## Canonical Sources

- Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11 (the Guru's final instructions)
- Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12 (the necessity of the Guru)
- Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.8 (the Guru who knows Brahman)
- Guru Gītā (Skanda Purāṇa)
- Bhagavad Gītā 4.34 (approach the Guru with humility)

# Om

## Canonical Name

Om

## Sanskrit

ॐ

## Transliteration

Om (also Auṃ)

## Śabda

ॐ

## Dhātu

अव् (Av) — To protect, to pervade. Some traditions derive Om from the root av (to protect) or from the three letters A-U-M representing creation, preservation, dissolution.

## Vyākaraṇa

Om is classified as a praṇava (primordial sound) and an avyaya (indeclinable). It is not declined like ordinary nouns. Pāṇini treats it as a sacred syllable (maṅgala-vācaka). The written form ॐ is a ligature of the three letters A, U, M with the anusvāra (nasal resonance) and the bindu (point of silence above).

## Nirukta

Yāska: Om is the name of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad: "Auṃ ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvam" — Om, this syllable is all this. The three letters represent the three states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep) and the three worlds.

## Bīja

ॐ itself is the mahā-bīja (great seed syllable) — the source of all other bīja mantras.

## Tattva

Praṇava-Tattva — the principle of the primordial sound. Om is the sonic form of Brahman — the vibration from which the universe emerges and into which it dissolves.

## Śakti

Nāda-Śakti — the power of primordial sound. Om is the first vibration of Śakti — the creative power of the universe expressed as sound.

## Literal Meaning

The primordial sound; the syllable of Brahman; yes; so be it; the affirmation of existence.

## Functional Meaning

Om is the sonic representation of Brahman — the absolute reality expressed as vibration. It is used as a prefix to all mantras, prayers, and sacred texts. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad teaches that Om encompasses all of time (past, present, future) and all states of consciousness. Meditation on Om leads to the direct experience of Brahman.

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta: Om = Brahman; meditating on Om is meditating on Brahman. In Mīmāṃsā: Om is the eternal, self-existent sound (śabda-brahman) — the Vedas are the eternal sound of Brahman. In Tantra: Om is the mahā-bīja from which all other bīja mantras emerge. In Yoga: Om is the name of Īśvara (God) — "tasya vācakaḥ praṇavaḥ" (Yoga Sūtras 1.27).

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: Om is the sound of the universe — the cosmic vibration (nāda-brahman) from which all creation emerges. The Purāṇas describe Brahmā creating the universe by uttering Om. The concept of nāda (sound) as the first manifestation of Brahman underlies the cosmological significance of Om.

## Psychology

Meditation on Om (Om-japa, Om-dhyāna) is the primary practice for stilling the mind. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad maps the four parts of Om (A, U, M, silence) onto the four states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep, turīya). The practice of Om-kāra-dhyāna (meditation on Om) leads through all four states to the recognition of Ātman = Brahman.

## Governance

Om as the foundation of governance: all royal proclamations and sacred oaths begin with Om. The concept of Om as the affirmation of cosmic order (ṛta) underlies its use in governance contexts.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Om is the primordial sound therapy. The vibration of Om is used in mantra-cikitsā (mantra therapy). Research suggests that chanting Om produces specific neurological effects — calming the nervous system and reducing stress.

## Mathematics

The concept of Om in mathematics: Om as the symbol of infinity (ananta) — the sound that contains all sounds. The bindu (point) above the Om symbol represents the mathematical point — dimensionless, yet the source of all dimensions.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Om is associated with the Sun (Sūrya) — the cosmic source of light and life. The Gāyatrī Mantra begins with Om and is addressed to the Sun. The concept of Om as the sound of the cosmic cycles (yugas, kalpas).

## Metallurgy

In ritual metallurgy: Om is inscribed on sacred objects to infuse them with divine power. The concept of Om as the mantra of consecration — all sacred metal objects are consecrated with Om.

## Ritual

Om begins and ends all Vedic rituals, mantras, and prayers. The Vedic tradition: "Om iti brahma" — Om is Brahman. The daily practice of Om-kāra-japa (repetition of Om) is the foundational spiritual practice. The concept of praṇava-upāsanā (worship through Om) is described in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

## Symbolism

The written symbol ॐ represents: A (waking state/creation), U (dreaming state/preservation), M (deep sleep/dissolution), the curve above (māyā/illusion), the dot (turīya/liberation), the silence after (Brahman). The three curves represent the three states of consciousness. The dot represents the fourth state (turīya) — pure awareness.

## Related Deities

- Brahman (Om is the sonic form of Brahman)
- Gaṇeśa (Om is associated with Gaṇeśa — "Om Gaṃ Gaṇapataye namaḥ")
- Śiva (Om Namaḥ Śivāya begins with Om)
- Viṣṇu (Om Namo Nārāyaṇāya begins with Om)

## Related Lokas

- All lokas are within Om — Om encompasses all of existence

## Related Koshas

- Om pervades all five koshas
- The silence after Om represents the Ātman beyond all koshas

## Related Chakras

- Sahasrāra (crown chakra) — the seat of Om's highest resonance
- Ājñā (third eye) — the seat of Om meditation
- Viśuddha (throat chakra) — the seat of Om's vocal expression

## Related Yantras

- Om Yantra (the written symbol ॐ is itself a yantra)
- Śrī Yantra (the visual equivalent of Om)

## Related Mantras

- Om is the prefix of all mantras
- Gāyatrī Mantra (begins with Om)
- Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra (begins with Om)
- "Om tat sat" (Bhagavad Gītā 17.23) — Om, That, Truth

## Related Vidyās

- Praṇava Vidyā (the science of Om — Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad)
- Nāda Vidyā (the science of sacred sound)
- Mantra Vidyā (all mantra science begins with Om)

## Related Śāstras

- Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad (dedicated entirely to Om)
- Yoga Sūtras 1.27-28 (Om as the name of Īśvara)
- Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1 (Om as the udgītha — the high chant)
- Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.8 (Om as Brahman)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta: Om = Brahman; the entire Upaniṣadic teaching is contained in Om
- Mīmāṃsā: Om is the eternal sound of the Vedas — śabda-brahman
- Yoga: Om is the name of Īśvara; japa of Om leads to samādhi
- Tantra: Om is the mahā-bīja — the source of all mantras and creation

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Om appears as a sacred affirmation
- Upaniṣadic period: Om systematized as the symbol of Brahman (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad)
- Classical period: Om as the universal prefix to all sacred utterances
- Tantric period: Om as the mahā-bīja of all mantra science
- Modern: Om as the universal symbol of Indian spirituality

## Cross References

- Brahman
- Nada (sacred sound)
- Mantra
- Samadhi
- Turiya (the fourth state of consciousness)

## Open Research Questions

- What is the neurological basis of Om's calming effect on the nervous system?
- How does the Vedic concept of Om as primordial sound relate to modern cosmological theories about the Big Bang as a primordial vibration?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some researchers propose that the frequency of Om chanting (approximately 136.1 Hz) corresponds to the Earth's resonant frequency (Schumann resonance). This remains under scientific investigation.

## Canonical Sources

- Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad (complete — dedicated to Om)
- Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1 (Om as the udgītha)
- Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.8.1 (Om as Brahman)
- Yoga Sūtras 1.27 (Om as the name of Īśvara)
- Bhagavad Gītā 17.23 (Om tat sat)

# Brahman

## Canonical Name

Brahman

## Sanskrit

ब्रह्मन्

## Transliteration

Brahman

## Śabda

ब्रह्मन्

## Dhātu

बृह् (Bṛh) — To expand, to grow, to be great.

## Vyākaraṇa

Brahman is a neuter noun (not to be confused with Brahmā, the masculine creator deity, or Brāhmaṇa, the priestly class). Derived from the root bṛh with the suffix -man. The neuter gender indicates that Brahman transcends all categories including gender.

## Nirukta

Yāska: "bṛhati iti brahma" — that which is great, that which expands. Brahman is the infinitely expanding reality that underlies all existence.

## Bīja

ॐ (Om/Auṃ) — the primordial sound that is the sonic form of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad opens: "Auṃ ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvam" — Om, this syllable is all this.

## Tattva

Brahma-Tattva — the principle of absolute, infinite, self-luminous reality. Brahman is described as Sat-Cit-Ānanda (Being-Consciousness-Bliss) — not three qualities but three aspects of one indivisible reality.

## Śakti

Brahman's śakti is Māyā — the creative power that projects the apparent multiplicity of the universe. In Śākta traditions, Brahman without Śakti is inert (śava); Brahman with Śakti is Śiva (the living absolute).

## Literal Meaning

The Absolute; the Infinite; the Ultimate Reality; the Ground of Being.

## Functional Meaning

Brahman is the infinite, eternal, unchanging absolute reality that is the ground of all existence. It is both the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) and the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) of the universe. Brahman is described via two approaches: Nirguṇa Brahman (without attributes — the absolute beyond all description) and Saguṇa Brahman (with attributes — the personal God, Īśvara). The Upaniṣads teach that Brahman is identical with Ātman (the individual Self).

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Brahman alone is real (Brahma satyam); the world is appearance (jagat mithyā); the individual self is Brahman (jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ). In Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Brahman is real, personal (Viṣṇu), and the universe and souls are Brahman's body. In Dvaita (Madhva): Brahman (Viṣṇu) is real and eternally distinct from souls and world. In Śaiva Siddhānta: Brahman is Śiva, the supreme reality with infinite śaktis.

## Cosmology

Brahman is the source, sustainer, and dissolution point of all universes. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante" — from which all beings are born, by which they live, into which they return — that is Brahman. The Purāṇas describe Brahman as the ocean from which the universe arises like waves. The concept of Brahmaṇḍa (Brahman's egg) is the cosmic egg from which the universe hatches.

## Psychology

Brahman as psychological reality: the deepest layer of consciousness is Brahman. In Yoga psychology, the state of samādhi (absorption) is the direct experience of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad identifies Brahman with the fourth state of consciousness (turīya) that underlies waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. The experience of Brahman is described as "neti neti" (not this, not this) — Brahman cannot be grasped by the mind but is the ground of the mind.

## Governance

The concept of Brahman in governance: the ideal ruler is one who has realized Brahman and governs from that realization. The Arthaśāstra's concept of the philosopher-king parallels the Upaniṣadic ideal of the Brahman-realized ruler. The concept of Brahma-rāṣṭra (the kingdom of Brahman) appears in Vedic literature as the ideal polity.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Brahman is the ultimate source of health (ārogya). The concept of Brahma-cakra (the cycle of Brahman) underlies the Āyurvedic understanding of the body as a microcosm of the universe. The highest healing is Brahma-jñāna (knowledge of Brahman) which removes the root cause of all disease — avidyā (ignorance).

## Mathematics

The concept of Brahman in mathematics: Brahman as the infinite (ananta) is the philosophical basis for the Indian mathematical concept of infinity. The concept of śūnya (zero) as the void from which all numbers emerge mirrors the Brahman-as-source concept. The Upaniṣadic statement "pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam" (that is full, this is full) is a mathematical statement about the nature of infinity.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Brahman is identified with the cosmic space (ākāśa) in which all celestial bodies move. The concept of Brahma-muhūrta (the hour of Brahman — 1.5 hours before sunrise) is the most auspicious time for spiritual practice. The Milky Way (Ākāśagaṅgā) is considered the visible form of Brahman's cosmic body.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: Brahman is the philosophical gold (parama-suvarṇa) — the ultimate substance that all metals aspire to become. The alchemical process of transmutation mirrors the spiritual process of realizing Brahman beneath the apparent multiplicity of substances.

## Ritual

The Brahma-yajña (sacrifice to Brahman) is the daily recitation of the Vedas — the highest ritual act. The Upanayana ceremony initiates the student into the study of Brahman. The Mahāvākyas are transmitted in ritual contexts as the direct teaching of Brahman. The concept of Brahma-vidyā (knowledge of Brahman) is the ultimate goal of all Vedic ritual.

## Symbolism

Om (ॐ) is the primary symbol of Brahman — the sound of the universe. The infinite space (ākāśa) symbolizes Brahman's all-pervading nature. The ocean symbolizes Brahman — waves (individual beings) arise from and return to the ocean. The sun symbolizes Nirguṇa Brahman — self-luminous, the source of all light. The bindu (point) in the center of a yantra represents Brahman as the source of all manifestation.

## Related Deities

- Brahman is not a deity but the ground of all deities
- Brahma (the creator) is Saguṇa Brahman's creative aspect
- Viṣṇu (the preserver) is Saguṇa Brahman's sustaining aspect
- Śiva (the destroyer) is Saguṇa Brahman's dissolving aspect
- Devī (the Goddess) is Brahman's Śakti — the dynamic aspect of the absolute

## Related Lokas

- Brahmaloka (Satyaloka) — the highest realm, closest to Brahman
- All lokas are within Brahman — "sarvam khalv idaṃ brahma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1)

## Related Koshas

- All five koshas are within Brahman
- Ānandamaya Kosha (bliss sheath) is the closest approximation to Brahman in the individual
- Beyond all koshas is Ātman = Brahman

## Related Chakras

- Sahasrāra (crown chakra) — the seat of Brahman realization in the individual body
- The entire chakra system is within Brahman

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (the geometric representation of Brahman's creative expansion)
- Bindu (the central point — Brahman as the source)

## Related Mantras

- "Aum" (the sonic form of Brahman)
- "Aham Brahmāsmi" (I am Brahman — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10)
- "Prajñānam Brahma" (Consciousness is Brahman — Aitareya Upaniṣad 3.3)
- "Sarvam khalv idaṃ brahma" (All this is indeed Brahman — Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1)

## Related Vidyās

- Brahmavidyā (knowledge of Brahman — the supreme vidyā)
- Ātmavidyā (self-knowledge = Brahmavidyā)
- Upaniṣad Vidyā (the teaching of the Upaniṣads)

## Related Śāstras

- Upaniṣads (primary source — especially Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Chāndogya, Taittirīya, Māṇḍūkya)
- Brahma Sūtras (Bādarāyaṇa — systematic exposition of Brahman)
- Bhagavad Gītā (Chapter 13 — Kṣetra-Kṣetrajña; Chapter 14 — Guṇatraya Vibhāga)
- Vivekacūḍāmaṇi (Śaṅkara)
- Brahma-Sūtra-Bhāṣya (Śaṅkara's commentary)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Brahman alone is real; world and individual self are appearances in Brahman
- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Brahman is personal (Viṣṇu); world and souls are Brahman's body
- Dvaita (Madhva): Brahman (Viṣṇu) is real and eternally distinct from souls and world
- Śaiva Siddhānta: Brahman is Śiva with infinite śaktis
- Śākta: Brahman is the Goddess (Devī) — the dynamic absolute
- Kashmir Śaivism: Brahman is Śiva-Śakti — pure consciousness and its creative power

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Brahman primarily means "sacred utterance" or "prayer power"
- Atharvaveda: Brahman as cosmic power
- Brāhmaṇa period: Brahman as the power of ritual
- Early Upaniṣads: Brahman as the ultimate reality, identical with Ātman
- Brahma Sūtras (200 BCE–200 CE): Systematic philosophy of Brahman
- Śaṅkara (8th century CE): Advaita — Brahman as the only reality
- Rāmānuja (11th century CE): Viśiṣṭādvaita — Brahman as personal God
- Madhva (13th century CE): Dvaita — Brahman as Viṣṇu, eternally distinct

## Cross References

- Atman
- Moksha
- Maya
- Ishvara (personal God as Saguṇa Brahman)
- Purusha
- Om

## Open Research Questions

- Is Nirguṇa Brahman (attributeless absolute) a coherent philosophical concept, or does it collapse into nothingness?
- How does the Advaita concept of Brahman relate to the Buddhist concept of śūnyatā (emptiness)?
- What is the relationship between Brahman and the modern cosmological concept of the quantum vacuum?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some physicists and philosophers propose that the quantum vacuum (the ground state of quantum field theory) has structural similarities to the Upaniṣadic concept of Brahman as the ground of all existence. This remains a philosophical analogy, not an established scientific or canonical claim.

## Canonical Sources

- Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1 (Brahman as the source of all)
- Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1 (Sarvam khalv idaṃ brahma)
- Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10 (Aham Brahmāsmi)
- Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad (Brahman as the four states of consciousness)
- Brahma Sūtras 1.1.1 (Athāto brahma-jijñāsā — now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman)

# Yajna

## Canonical Name

Yajna

## Sanskrit

यज्ञ

## Transliteration

Yajña

## Śabda

यज्ञ

## Dhātu

यज् (Yaj) — To worship, to sacrifice, to offer.

## Vyākaraṇa

Yajña is a masculine noun derived from the root yaj (to worship/sacrifice) with the suffix -na. The root yaj is one of the most important roots in Vedic Sanskrit — it gives yajña (sacrifice), yajus (sacrificial formula), yajamāna (sacrificer), and Yajurveda (the Veda of sacrificial formulas).

## Nirukta

Yāska: "yajyate devā anena iti yajñaḥ" — that by which the gods are worshipped. Yajña is the act of offering that creates and maintains the relationship between humans and the divine.

## Bīja

ॐ (Om) — the primordial offering. Also स्वाहा (Svāhā) — the mantra of offering in fire rituals.

## Tattva

Yajña-Tattva — the principle of sacred exchange and cosmic reciprocity. The universe itself is a yajña — a continuous cycle of giving and receiving between all levels of existence.

## Śakti

Yajña-Śakti — the power of sacred offering. The śakti that maintains the cosmic order through the cycle of giving.

## Literal Meaning

Sacrifice; offering; worship; the sacred act of giving.

## Functional Meaning

Yajña is the foundational principle of Vedic civilization — the sacred act of offering that maintains cosmic order (ṛta). The Bhagavad Gītā (3.10-16) describes yajña as the cosmic cycle: Brahmā created beings along with yajña; through yajña, rain falls; from rain, food grows; from food, beings live; beings perform yajña — the wheel of cosmic reciprocity. Yajña operates at five levels: Brahma-yajña (study of Vedas), Deva-yajña (fire offerings to gods), Pitṛ-yajña (offerings to ancestors), Bhūta-yajña (offerings to all beings), Manuṣya-yajña (hospitality to humans).

## Ontology

In Mīmāṃsā: yajña is the primary means of achieving all human goals — dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. The apūrva (unseen potency) of yajña persists until it bears fruit. In Advaita: yajña at the highest level is the offering of the ego into the fire of knowledge (jñāna-yajña). In the Bhagavad Gītā: karma-yoga is yajña — all action performed without attachment is an offering to the divine.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: the universe itself was created through a cosmic yajña — the Puruṣa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90) describes the primordial sacrifice of the cosmic Puruṣa from which all creation emerged. The concept of yajña as the mechanism of cosmic maintenance — the gods depend on yajña for their sustenance.

## Psychology

Yajña as psychological principle: the offering of the ego (ahaṃkāra) into the fire of self-knowledge is the highest yajña. The Bhagavad Gītā (4.24-33) describes multiple forms of yajña as psychological practices: offering the senses into the fire of restraint, offering actions into the fire of knowledge.

## Governance

Rāja-sūya (royal consecration) and Aśvamedha (horse sacrifice) are the primary royal yajñas. The king's yajña maintains the prosperity of the kingdom. The concept of rāṣṭra-yajña (national sacrifice) — governance as a form of yajña for the welfare of all.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: yajña smoke (dhūpa) is used for purification and healing. The concept of yajña as environmental medicine — fire offerings purify the atmosphere. Modern research on yajña smoke (homa therapy) suggests antimicrobial properties.

## Mathematics

The Śulbasūtras (altar-building manuals) contain the earliest known mathematical theorems, developed for constructing yajña altars of precise areas. The Pythagorean theorem, geometric transformations, and irrational numbers appear in the context of yajña altar construction.

## Astronomy

The timing of yajñas is determined by Jyotiṣa (Vedic astronomy). The concept of muhūrta (auspicious time) for yajña is based on astronomical calculations. The Nakṣatra system was developed partly for determining the correct times for yajña.

## Metallurgy

The sacred fire (agni) of yajña is the basis of all metallurgical fire. The concept of dhātu-yajña (offering of metals) — specific metals are offered in specific yajñas for specific results.

## Ritual

The five mahāyajñas (great sacrifices): Brahma-yajña, Deva-yajña, Pitṛ-yajña, Bhūta-yajña, Manuṣya-yajña. The Soma yajña (Agniṣṭoma, Vājapeya, Rājasūya) are the major Vedic sacrifices. The agnihotra (daily fire offering) is the minimal yajña obligation.

## Symbolism

The fire symbolizes yajña — the transformative medium of offering. The smoke rising from the fire symbolizes the offering reaching the divine realm. The svāhā (offering mantra) symbolizes the act of giving without reservation.

## Related Deities

- Agni (the fire deity — the medium of yajña)
- Indra (the primary recipient of Soma offerings)
- Viṣṇu (Yajña is one of Viṣṇu's names — he is the cosmic sacrifice)
- Brahmā (the creator who established yajña)

## Related Lokas

- Svarga (heaven — the destination of yajña's merit)
- Pitṛloka (the realm of ancestors — maintained by Pitṛ-yajña)

## Related Koshas

- Prāṇamaya Kosha (energy sheath) — the field of prāṇa-yajña (offering of breath)
- Annamaya Kosha (physical sheath) — the field of physical offerings

## Related Chakras

- Maṇipūra (solar plexus) — the fire chakra; the seat of the inner yajña
- Anāhata (heart chakra) — the seat of bhakti-yajña (devotional offering)

## Related Yantras

- Agni Yantra (the triangular yantra of the fire offering)

## Related Mantras

- "Svāhā" (the offering mantra)
- Puruṣa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90 — the cosmic sacrifice)
- Gāyatrī Mantra (the mantra of the solar yajña)

## Related Vidyās

- Yajña Vidyā (the science of sacred offering)
- Śulbasūtra Vidyā (the geometry of yajña altars)

## Related Śāstras

- Ṛgveda (Puruṣa Sūkta 10.90)
- Yajurveda (the Veda of sacrificial formulas)
- Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (the most detailed text on yajña)
- Bhagavad Gītā 3.10-16, 4.24-33 (yajña as cosmic principle and yoga)
- Śulbasūtras (yajña altar geometry)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Mīmāṃsā: Yajña is the primary means of achieving all human goals
- Advaita: Jñāna-yajña (offering of knowledge) is the highest yajña
- Bhagavad Gītā: All action performed without attachment is yajña

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Yajña as the primary religious act
- Brāhmaṇa period: Elaborate yajña rituals developed
- Upaniṣadic period: Yajña internalized as psychological practice
- Bhagavad Gītā: Yajña as the cosmic principle of selfless action
- Modern: Yajña as environmental ritual and community practice

## Cross References

- Agni
- Dharma
- Karma
- Prana
- Rta

## Open Research Questions

- What is the environmental impact of large-scale yajña? Does homa therapy have measurable antimicrobial effects?
- How does the Vedic concept of yajña as cosmic reciprocity relate to modern ecological concepts of circular economy?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some researchers propose that the smoke from specific yajña herbs (agnihotra) has measurable antimicrobial and air-purifying properties. Preliminary studies suggest this, but rigorous scientific validation is ongoing.

## Canonical Sources

- Ṛgveda 10.90 (Puruṣa Sūkta — the cosmic sacrifice)
- Bhagavad Gītā 3.10-16 (yajña as cosmic cycle)
- Bhagavad Gītā 4.24-33 (the many forms of yajña)
- Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (detailed yajña procedures)
- Śulbasūtras (yajña altar geometry)

# Ahimsa

## Canonical Name

Ahimsa

## Sanskrit

अहिंसा

## Transliteration

Ahimsa

## Literal Meaning

Non-violence; non-harm; non-injury. From Sanskrit a (not) + himsa (violence, harm, injury).

## Ahimsa Paramo Dharma

The phrase **Ahimsa Paramo Dharma** (अहिंसा परमो धर्मः) means:

**"Non-violence is the highest dharma."**

- Ahimsa = non-violence
- Paramo = highest, supreme
- Dharma = duty, righteousness, cosmic order

This maxim appears in the Mahabharata (Anushasana Parva 115.1) and is one of the most cited ethical statements in Indian tradition. The full verse continues: "Ahimsa paramo dharma, tatha ahimsa paramo tapah" — Non-violence is the highest dharma; non-violence is the highest austerity.

## Functional Meaning

Ahimsa is the principle of not causing harm to any living being — in thought, word, or action. It is the foundational ethical principle shared across Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist traditions. In Jainism, ahimsa is the first and supreme vow. In Yoga, ahimsa is the first of the five Yamas (ethical restraints) in Patanjali's Ashtanga Yoga. In the Mahabharata, ahimsa is declared the highest dharma.

## Marathi Summary

अहिंसा म्हणजे विचार, शब्द किंवा कृतीतून कोणत्याही सजीवाला इजा न करणे. जैन परंपरेत ती सर्वोच्च व्रत मानली जाते.

## Jain Teaching on Ahimsa

The Acharanga Sutra (the oldest Jain canonical text) states the core teaching of ahimsa:

"All beings desire to live. None wishes to die. Therefore, a wise person does not kill, nor causes others to kill, nor consents to killing."

The Five Great Vows (Mahavrata) for Jain monks place Ahimsa first:
1. Ahimsa — Non-violence toward all living beings
2. Satya — Absolute truthfulness
3. Asteya — Non-stealing
4. Brahmacharya — Celibacy
5. Aparigraha — Complete non-possessiveness

UniGuru Citation: Acharanga Sutra, Book 1, Lecture 7; Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22, Jacobi translation

## Yoga Teaching on Ahimsa

In Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (2.30), Ahimsa is the first of the five Yamas:
"Ahimsa-satya-asteya-brahmacharya-aparigraha yamah" — Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the five restraints.

Patanjali states (Yoga Sutras 2.35): "Ahimsa-pratishthayam tat-sannidhau vaira-tyagah" — When one is established in non-violence, all enmity is abandoned in one's presence.

## Dharma Connection

The Mahabharata (Anushasana Parva) states: "Ahimsa paramo dharma" — Non-violence is the highest dharma. The Caraka Samhita (Ayurvedic text) states that the physician's svadharma includes ahimsa (non-harm) as the first ethical principle. Dharma.md cross-references Ahimsa as a related concept.

## Cosmology and Ethics

Ahimsa operates at multiple levels:
- Physical: not harming the body of any being
- Verbal: not speaking words that harm
- Mental: not harboring harmful thoughts

In Jain cosmology, every act of violence (himsa) generates karma that binds the soul. Ahimsa is therefore both an ethical principle and a metaphysical necessity for liberation (moksha).

## Related Concepts

- Dharma (Ahimsa paramo dharma — non-violence is the highest dharma)
- Karma (violence generates binding karma)
- Moksha (ahimsa is necessary for liberation)
- Satya (truth — the second great vow, companion to ahimsa)
- Yoga (ahimsa is the first Yama in Patanjali's system)

## Related Shastras

- Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva (primary source for "Ahimsa paramo dharma")
- Acharanga Sutra (Jain canonical source — oldest text on ahimsa)
- Yoga Sutras of Patanjali (2.30 — ahimsa as first Yama)
- Caraka Samhita (Ayurvedic ethics — ahimsa as physician's duty)
- Tattvartha Sutra (Jain systematic philosophy of ahimsa)

## Canonical Sources

- Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva 115.1: "Ahimsa paramo dharma"
- Acharanga Sutra, Book 1, Lecture 7 (Jain canonical teaching)
- Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 2.30 (ahimsa as first Yama)
- Caraka Samhita Sutrasthana 1.15 (physician's dharma includes ahimsa)

UniGuru Citation: Mahabharata Anushasana Parva; Acharanga Sutra; Yoga Sutras of Patanjali

# Moksha

## Canonical Name

Moksha

## Sanskrit

मोक्ष

## Transliteration

Mokṣa

## Śabda

मोक्ष

## Dhātu

मुच् (Muc) — To release, to free, to liberate.

## Vyākaraṇa

Mokṣa is a masculine noun derived from the root muc (to release) with the suffix -a. Related forms: mukti (liberation), vimokṣa (complete liberation), apavarga (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika term for liberation).

## Nirukta

"Mucyate iti mokṣaḥ" — that from which one is released, or the state of being released. Liberation from the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra) and from the bondage of ignorance (avidyā).

## Bīja

ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the bīja of liberation in Śākta traditions. Also ॐ (Om) as the sound of the liberated state.

## Tattva

Mokṣa-Tattva — the principle of ultimate liberation. The fourth and highest Puruṣārtha (aim of human life), transcending Dharma, Artha, and Kāma. In Advaita: Mokṣa is the recognition of what always already is — Ātman = Brahman. In Sāṃkhya: Mokṣa is the Puruṣa's recognition of its eternal distinction from Prakṛti (kaivalya).

## Śakti

Mukti-Śakti — the liberating power. In Śākta traditions, the Goddess grants mokṣa through her grace (anugraha-śakti). In Vaiṣṇava traditions, Viṣṇu's grace (prasāda) is the liberating power.

## Literal Meaning

Liberation; release; freedom from bondage.

## Functional Meaning

Mokṣa is freedom from the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth (saṃsāra) and from the root cause of that cycle — ignorance (avidyā) and its product, ego (ahaṃkāra). It is not a place or a future state but the recognition of one's true nature as already free. The Upaniṣads teach that bondage and liberation are both appearances — the Ātman was never bound. Different schools describe mokṣa differently: as jīvanmukti (liberation while living), videhamukti (liberation at death), sāyujya (union with God), sālokya (dwelling in God's realm), sārūpya (having God's form), sāmīpya (proximity to God).

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta: Mokṣa is the removal of the superimposition (adhyāsa) of non-self on the Self. It is not an achievement but a recognition. Jīvanmukti (liberation while living) is possible. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: Mokṣa is eternal service to Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha — the soul retains its individuality. In Dvaita: Mokṣa is eternal blissful service to Viṣṇu — the soul never merges with Brahman. In Sāṃkhya: Kaivalya (aloneness) — Puruṣa rests in its own nature, free from Prakṛti's entanglement. In Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika: Apavarga — the cessation of all pain and pleasure; a state of pure existence without consciousness (controversial).

## Cosmology

In Purāṇic cosmology: liberated souls (muktas) dwell in Brahmaloka (Satyaloka) until the final dissolution (mahāpralaya), after which they merge with Brahman. In Vaiṣṇava cosmology: liberated souls dwell eternally in Vaikuṇṭha (Viṣṇu's realm) or Goloka (Kṛṣṇa's realm). In Śaiva cosmology: liberated souls merge with Śiva or dwell in Śivaloka. The concept of krama-mukti (gradual liberation) describes the soul's journey through higher realms before final liberation.

## Psychology

Mokṣa as psychological state: the liberated person (jīvanmukta) lives in the world but is not bound by it. The Yoga Vāsiṣṭha describes the psychology of liberation in detail: the liberated mind is like a burnt rope — it retains its form but has no binding power. The characteristics of a jīvanmukta include: equanimity (samatvam), freedom from desire (vairāgya), compassion (karuṇā), and spontaneous right action (sahaja-karma).

## Governance

The concept of mokṣa in governance: the ideal ruler seeks mokṣa through dharmic governance. The Arthaśāstra acknowledges mokṣa as the ultimate goal even for kings. The concept of rāja-ṛṣi (royal sage) — a king who governs while pursuing liberation — is the Vedic ideal. Janaka (king of Videha) is the paradigmatic example of a ruler who achieved mokṣa while governing.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: mokṣa is the ultimate health — freedom from all disease at the root level. The concept of mokṣa-dharma in Āyurveda: the physician's highest service is to guide patients toward liberation. The Caraka Saṃhitā states that the ultimate aim of Āyurveda is not just physical health but mokṣa.

## Mathematics

The concept of mokṣa in mathematics: liberation from the cycle of saṃsāra mirrors the mathematical concept of escaping an infinite series. The concept of ananta (infinity) in Indian mathematics is connected to the infinite nature of the liberated state. The Upaniṣadic statement "pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam" (that is full, this is full) describes the mathematical completeness of the liberated state.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: the 12th house (vyaya bhāva) in the birth chart represents mokṣa. The nakṣatra Abhijit is associated with mokṣa. The concept of uttarāyaṇa (the sun's northward journey) is associated with the path of liberation (devayāna) in the Upaniṣads.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: mokṣa is the alchemical gold — the final transmutation of the base metal of ego into the pure gold of liberated consciousness. The Rasaśāstra tradition treats the alchemical process as a metaphor for spiritual liberation.

## Ritual

The Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra is the primary ritual for liberation from the death-cycle. The Śrāddha ritual is performed to assist the departed soul on its journey toward mokṣa. The Kāśī (Varanasi) pilgrimage is considered a direct path to mokṣa — dying in Kāśī is believed to grant liberation. The Gāyatrī Mantra is considered a mokṣa-mantra when understood at its deepest level.

## Symbolism

The open sky (ākāśa) symbolizes mokṣa — boundless, free, uncontained. The bird in flight symbolizes the liberated soul. The lotus rising from mud symbolizes mokṣa — purity emerging from worldly existence. The extinguished flame (nirvāṇa) symbolizes mokṣa in Buddhist tradition. The open door symbolizes mokṣa — the passage from bondage to freedom.

## Related Deities

- Viṣṇu (the liberator — grants mokṣa through grace)
- Śiva (Maheśvara — the great lord who grants liberation)
- Devī (Tārā — the Goddess who carries across the ocean of saṃsāra)
- Yama (Dharmarāja — the lord who oversees the transition to liberation)
- Gaṇeśa (the remover of obstacles on the path to mokṣa)

## Related Lokas

- Brahmaloka (Satyaloka) — the realm of liberation
- Vaikuṇṭha (Viṣṇu's realm — Vaiṣṇava mokṣa)
- Kailāsa (Śiva's realm — Śaiva mokṣa)
- Goloka (Kṛṣṇa's realm — highest Vaiṣṇava mokṣa)

## Related Koshas

- Beyond all five koshas is the liberated Ātman
- The dissolution of identification with all koshas is mokṣa
- Ānandamaya Kosha (bliss sheath) is the last veil before mokṣa

## Related Chakras

- Sahasrāra (crown chakra) — the chakra of liberation; when kuṇḍalinī reaches here, mokṣa is attained
- Brahmarandhra (the aperture at the crown) — the exit point of the liberated soul

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (the yantra of liberation through the Goddess)
- Mṛtyuñjaya Yantra (for liberation from the death-cycle)

## Related Mantras

- Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra (liberation from death)
- "Om namo bhagavate vāsudevāya" (Vaiṣṇava liberation mantra)
- "Om namaḥ śivāya" (Śaiva liberation mantra)
- "Aham Brahmāsmi" (the mantra of Advaita liberation)

## Related Vidyās

- Brahmavidyā (knowledge of Brahman = mokṣa)
- Ātmavidyā (self-knowledge = mokṣa)
- Mokṣa-Dharma Vidyā (the science of liberation — Mahābhārata Śāntiparva)

## Related Śāstras

- Upaniṣads (primary source)
- Bhagavad Gītā (the entire text is a teaching on mokṣa)
- Brahma Sūtras
- Yoga Sūtras (kaivalya = mokṣa)
- Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (psychology of liberation)
- Vivekacūḍāmaṇi (Śaṅkara)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta: Mokṣa is the recognition of Ātman = Brahman; jīvanmukti is possible
- Viśiṣṭādvaita: Mokṣa is eternal service to Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha; soul retains individuality
- Dvaita: Mokṣa is eternal blissful service to Viṣṇu; soul never merges with Brahman
- Sāṃkhya: Kaivalya — Puruṣa rests in its own nature, free from Prakṛti
- Buddhism: Nirvāṇa — the extinguishing of craving, aversion, and delusion
- Jainism: Mokṣa — the soul (jīva) freed from all karma, dwelling at the top of the universe (Siddhashila)

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: No explicit mokṣa concept; immortality (amṛtatva) is the goal
- Upaniṣadic period: Mokṣa as liberation from saṃsāra established
- Buddhist period: Nirvāṇa as the Buddhist equivalent of mokṣa
- Jain period: Mokṣa as the soul's liberation from karma-matter
- Epic-Purāṇic period: Mokṣa as the fourth Puruṣārtha; various paths described
- Medieval bhakti: Mokṣa through devotion (bhakti) — accessible to all
- Modern: Mokṣa reinterpreted as psychological liberation, social liberation, ecological liberation

## Cross References

- Dharma
- Karma
- Atman
- Brahman
- Yoga
- Nirvana (Buddhist equivalent)
- Kaivalya (Sāṃkhya-Yoga equivalent)
- Mukti (synonym)

## Open Research Questions

- Is jīvanmukti (liberation while living) a coherent concept? Can a person be liberated and still act in the world?
- What is the relationship between mokṣa and nirvāṇa? Are they the same state described differently?
- Can mokṣa be understood as a psychological state achievable through contemplative practice, independent of metaphysical claims?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some researchers propose that the neurological correlates of deep meditation states (samādhi) may correspond to the psychological dimension of mokṣa. This remains a scientific hypothesis and does not constitute canonical teaching.

## Canonical Sources

- Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.3-4 (the chariot metaphor for liberation)
- Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8 (the liberated soul merges with Brahman)
- Bhagavad Gītā 18.66 (sarva-dharmān parityajya — surrender and be liberated)
- Yoga Sūtras 4.34 (kaivalya — the final liberation)
- Mahābhārata Śāntiparva (Mokṣadharma section)

# Prana

## Canonical Name

Prana

## Sanskrit

प्राण

## Transliteration

Prāṇa

## Śabda

प्राण

## Dhātu

प्र + अन् (Pra + An) — Pra (forward, forth) + An (to breathe, to live). That which breathes forth; the forward-moving breath.

## Vyākaraṇa

Prāṇa is a masculine noun. The prefix pra- (forward) combined with the root an- (to breathe) gives prāṇa — the primary, forward-moving life-breath. Distinguished from the five vāyus: Prāṇa (inward breath), Apāna (downward breath), Samāna (equalizing breath), Udāna (upward breath), Vyāna (pervading breath).

## Nirukta

"Prāṇiti iti prāṇaḥ" — that which breathes is prāṇa. The life-force that animates all living beings.

## Bīja

यं (Yaṃ) — the bīja of vāyu (air/wind), the element most closely associated with prāṇa. Also हं (Haṃ) — the bīja of the throat chakra (Viśuddha) associated with prāṇa's vocal expression.

## Tattva

Prāṇa-Tattva — the life-force principle. Prāṇa is the bridge between the physical body (annamaya kosha) and the mind (manomaya kosha). It is the animating principle that distinguishes the living from the dead.

## Śakti

Prāṇa-Śakti — the vital power. The śakti that animates all living beings. In Śākta traditions, prāṇa-śakti is the Goddess's life-giving power manifest in every breath.

## Literal Meaning

Breath; life-force; vital energy; the animating principle.

## Functional Meaning

Prāṇa is the universal life-force that animates all living beings. It operates through the prāṇamaya kosha (energy sheath) and the network of nāḍīs (energy channels). The five prāṇas (pañca-vāyu) govern specific physiological functions: Prāṇa (respiration, heart), Apāna (elimination, reproduction), Samāna (digestion, assimilation), Udāna (speech, upward movement, death), Vyāna (circulation, distribution). Prāṇāyāma (breath control) is the primary yogic practice for working with prāṇa.

## Ontology

In Vedic ontology: Prāṇa is the cosmic life-force — "prāṇo vai brahma" (Prāṇa is indeed Brahman — Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad). In Sāṃkhya: Prāṇa is the activity of the subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra). In Advaita: Prāṇa is the manifestation of Brahman as the life-force. In Āyurveda: Prāṇa is the primary vāta-doṣa — the governing principle of all movement and nervous function.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: Prāṇa is the cosmic breath — the universe breathes in and out through cosmic cycles (kalpa). The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad describes a cosmic debate among the prāṇas to determine which is supreme — prāṇa (breath) wins because when it leaves, all other faculties cease. In Purāṇic cosmology: Prāṇa is the breath of Brahma — the universe is created on his outbreath and dissolved on his inbreath.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology: prāṇa and mind (manas) are intimately connected — "prāṇe manaḥ" (the mind is in prāṇa). Controlling prāṇa through prāṇāyāma controls the mind. The concept of prāṇa-spanda (the vibration of prāṇa) in Kashmir Śaivism is the basis of all mental activity. The five prāṇas govern different psychological functions: Prāṇa (attention, perception), Apāna (letting go, release), Samāna (integration, balance), Udāna (aspiration, will), Vyāna (expansion, connection).

## Governance

The concept of prāṇa in governance: the king's prāṇa (vitality) is the prāṇa of the kingdom. The Arthaśāstra prescribes prāṇāyāma and yoga for the ruler's mental clarity. The concept of rāṣṭra-prāṇa (the life-force of the nation) appears in political philosophy.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Prāṇa is the primary vāta-doṣa governing the nervous system, respiration, and all movement. Prāṇa-vāyu specifically governs the heart and respiratory system. Prāṇa imbalance is the root of all vāta disorders. Prāṇāyāma is the primary Āyurvedic therapy for prāṇa disorders. The concept of prāṇa-pratīkāra (prāṇa therapy) includes breath work, marma therapy, and yoga.

## Mathematics

The concept of prāṇa in mathematics: the Vedic concept of prāṇa as the animating principle of numbers — each number has its own prāṇa (vitality). The concept of prāṇa in Vedic meter (chandas): each meter has a specific prāṇa (breath pattern) that gives it its power.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Prāṇa is associated with the Sun (Sūrya) — the cosmic prāṇa-source. The concept of prāṇa-āyuṣa (life-span calculation) in Jyotiṣa uses prāṇa as the unit of time. The prāṇa (a unit of time = 4 seconds) is the smallest unit in Vedic time measurement.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: prāṇa is the life-force that must be infused into alchemical preparations. The concept of prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā (installation of life-force) in idol-making is the ritual infusion of prāṇa into a metal image. Mercury (pārada) is considered the prāṇa of metals in Rasaśāstra.

## Ritual

Prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā (installation of life-force) is the ritual that animates a deity's image. The prāṇāyāma performed before ritual purifies the prāṇa of the practitioner. The concept of prāṇa-āhuti (offering of prāṇa) in yajña — the breath itself is offered to the fire.

## Symbolism

The breath symbolizes prāṇa — the most immediate experience of life-force. The wind (vāyu) symbolizes prāṇa's invisible, pervading nature. The serpent (nāga) symbolizes prāṇa's movement through the nāḍīs. The lotus symbolizes prāṇa's blooming in the heart.

## Related Deities

- Vāyu (the wind deity — the cosmic form of prāṇa)
- Indra (the lord of prāṇa in the Upaniṣads)
- Hanumān (the son of Vāyu — the embodiment of prāṇa-śakti)
- Prāṇa-devī (the Goddess as life-force)

## Related Lokas

- Vāyu-loka (the realm of wind/prāṇa)
- All lokas are sustained by prāṇa

## Related Koshas

- Prāṇamaya Kosha (energy sheath) — the primary domain of prāṇa
- Annamaya Kosha (physical sheath) — animated by prāṇa
- Manomaya Kosha (mind sheath) — connected to prāṇa through breath

## Related Chakras

- Anāhata (heart chakra) — the seat of prāṇa-vāyu
- Viśuddha (throat chakra) — the seat of udāna-vāyu
- Svādhiṣṭhāna (sacral chakra) — the seat of apāna-vāyu
- Maṇipūra (solar plexus) — the seat of samāna-vāyu

## Related Yantras

- Vāyu Yantra (hexagonal — the geometric form of the air element)
- Prāṇa Yantra (for prāṇa healing practices)

## Related Mantras

- "So'ham" (I am That) — the natural mantra of the breath (So = inhalation, Ham = exhalation)
- "Prāṇāya svāhā" (offering to prāṇa — from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad)
- Prāṇa Gāyatrī: "Om prāṇāya vidmahe vāyudevāya dhīmahi"

## Related Vidyās

- Prāṇāyāma Vidyā (science of breath control)
- Prāṇa-Vidyā (science of life-force — Upaniṣadic teaching)
- Marma Vidyā (science of vital points — prāṇa junctions in the body)

## Related Śāstras

- Praśna Upaniṣad (dedicated to the teaching of prāṇa)
- Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1 (the debate of the prāṇas)
- Yoga Sūtras 2.49-53 (prāṇāyāma)
- Caraka Saṃhitā (prāṇa in Āyurveda)
- Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā (prāṇāyāma techniques)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Vedic: Prāṇa is Brahman — the cosmic life-force
- Āyurvedic: Prāṇa is the primary vāta-doṣa — the governing principle of all movement
- Yogic: Prāṇa is the bridge between body and mind — controlling prāṇa controls the mind
- Tantric: Prāṇa is the vehicle of consciousness — where prāṇa goes, consciousness follows

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Prāṇa as breath and life
- Upaniṣadic period: Prāṇa as cosmic life-force and Brahman
- Āyurvedic period: Prāṇa systematized as the five vāyus
- Yogic period: Prāṇāyāma developed as a systematic practice
- Tantric period: Prāṇa as the vehicle of kuṇḍalinī-śakti

## Cross References

- Yoga
- Atman
- Agni
- Kosha (Prāṇamaya Kosha)
- Chakra (Anāhata)
- Vata (Āyurvedic dosha)

## Open Research Questions

- What is the relationship between prāṇa and the modern concept of bioelectricity?
- How do the five prāṇas (pañca-vāyu) map onto modern physiological systems?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some researchers propose that prāṇa corresponds to the bioelectric field that surrounds and permeates living organisms. This remains under scientific investigation and is not established canon.

## Canonical Sources

- Praśna Upaniṣad (complete — dedicated to prāṇa)
- Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1-14 (the debate of the prāṇas)
- Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.11 (prāṇa as the highest)
- Yoga Sūtras 2.49-53 (prāṇāyāma)
- Caraka Saṃhitā Sūtrasthāna 12 (prāṇa in Āyurveda)
