# Akasha

## Canonical Name

Akasha

## Sanskrit

आकाश

## Transliteration

Ākāśa

## Śabda

आकाश

## Dhātu

आ + काश् (Ā + Kāś) — Ā (towards, completely) + Kāś (to shine, to be luminous). That which shines completely; the luminous space.

## Vyākaraṇa

Ākāśa is a masculine noun derived from the prefix ā- and the root kāś (to shine). The word conveys both the sense of "space" and "luminosity" — space is not empty but luminous.

## Nirukta

"Ākāśate iti ākāśaḥ" — that which shines. Space is not mere emptiness but the luminous ground of all existence.

## Bīja

हं (Haṃ) — the bīja of the space element (ākāśa) in Tantric traditions. Associated with the Viśuddha chakra (throat — the space center).

## Tattva

Ākāśa-Tattva — the space principle. The first and subtlest of the five mahābhūtas (great elements): Ākāśa (space), Vāyu (air), Agni (fire), Āp (water), Pṛthvī (earth). Ākāśa is the substratum of all other elements — they all exist within space.

## Śakti

Ākāśa-Śakti — the power of infinite space. The śakti that provides the ground for all manifestation. In Tantric traditions, ākāśa is the śakti of pure potentiality.

## Literal Meaning

Space; ether; sky; the luminous void.

## Functional Meaning

Ākāśa is the subtlest of the five elements — the space in which all other elements and all phenomena exist. It is the medium of sound (śabda) — sound travels through ākāśa. In Vedānta, ākāśa is the first element to emerge from Brahman in the process of creation. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad teaches that Brahman is ākāśa — the infinite space of consciousness.

## Ontology

In Vaiśeṣika: Ākāśa is one of the nine dravyas (substances) — it is eternal, all-pervading, and the substratum of sound. In Advaita: Ākāśa is the first manifestation of Brahman — "ākāśo ha vai nāma nāmarūpayor nirvahitā" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1). In Sāṃkhya: Ākāśa is the first tanmātra (subtle element) — śabda-tanmātra (sound-essence) — from which the gross space element emerges.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: Ākāśa is the first element created — from Brahman comes ākāśa, from ākāśa comes vāyu, from vāyu comes agni, from agni comes āp, from āp comes pṛthvī (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1). The concept of cidākāśa (consciousness-space) — the infinite space of pure awareness that is Brahman.

## Psychology

Ākāśa as psychological principle: the mind (manas) is like ākāśa — it provides the space in which thoughts arise and dissolve. The concept of cidākāśa (consciousness-space) — the pure awareness that is the ground of all mental activity. The practice of ākāśa-dhāraṇā (concentration on space) leads to the experience of infinite consciousness.

## Governance

The concept of ākāśa in governance: the ruler who governs from the space of ākāśa (non-attachment, equanimity) governs wisely. The concept of rāja-ākāśa (the space of the king) — the king's court as the space where all voices are heard.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Ākāśa is the element associated with the vāta doṣa (along with vāyu). The concept of ākāśa in the body: the spaces within the body (channels, cavities) are the body's ākāśa. Ākāśa imbalance leads to vāta disorders — anxiety, dryness, instability.

## Mathematics

The concept of ākāśa in mathematics: the concept of infinite space (ananta-ākāśa) is the philosophical basis for the Indian mathematical concept of infinity. The concept of śūnya (zero) as the mathematical ākāśa — the empty space from which all numbers emerge.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Ākāśa is the space in which all celestial bodies move. The concept of ākāśa-gaṅgā (the Milky Way — the river of space). The nakṣatra system maps the ākāśa into 27 divisions.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: ākāśa is the space in which alchemical transformations occur. The concept of ākāśa as the medium of subtle influences — the alchemist works with the ākāśa of the laboratory.

## Ritual

The concept of ākāśa in ritual: the ritual space (yajña-śālā) is a consecrated ākāśa — a space set apart from ordinary space. The concept of maṇḍala (sacred circle) as a bounded ākāśa. The concept of ākāśa-dīpa (sky lamp) — a lamp offered to the infinite space.

## Symbolism

The sky (ākāśa) symbolizes infinite space, freedom, and the divine. The blue color symbolizes ākāśa — the sky's color. The void (śūnya) symbolizes ākāśa's nature as the ground of all existence. The mirror symbolizes ākāśa — it reflects all without being affected.

## Related Deities

- Viṣṇu (Vaikuṇṭha — Viṣṇu's realm is the highest ākāśa)
- Śiva (Cidambaram — the space of consciousness — Śiva's primary form is ākāśa)
- Indra (the lord of the sky — the cosmic ākāśa)

## Related Lokas

- All lokas exist within ākāśa
- Brahmaloka (the highest ākāśa — the space of Brahman)

## Related Koshas

- All five koshas exist within ākāśa
- Ānandamaya Kosha (bliss sheath) — the subtlest kosha, closest to ākāśa

## Related Chakras

- Viśuddha (throat chakra) — the ākāśa chakra; the seat of space and sound
- Sahasrāra (crown chakra) — the infinite ākāśa of pure consciousness

## Related Yantras

- Ākāśa Yantra (circular — the circle represents infinite space)

## Related Mantras

- "Haṃ" (the bīja of ākāśa)
- "Sarvam khalv idaṃ brahma" (All this is Brahman — the ākāśa of Brahman)

## Related Vidyās

- Ākāśa Vidyā (the science of space — Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14)
- Cidākāśa Vidyā (the science of consciousness-space)

## Related Śāstras

- Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1 (ākāśa as the first element)
- Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14 (Brahman as ākāśa)
- Vaiśeṣika Sūtras (ākāśa as a substance)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Vaiśeṣika: Ākāśa is an eternal, all-pervading substance — the substratum of sound
- Advaita: Ākāśa is the first manifestation of Brahman; cidākāśa (consciousness-space) is Brahman itself
- Sāṃkhya: Ākāśa emerges from the śabda-tanmātra (sound-essence)

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Ākāśa as the sky and cosmic space
- Upaniṣadic period: Ākāśa as the first element and as Brahman
- Vaiśeṣika period: Ākāśa systematized as one of nine substances
- Tantric period: Ākāśa as the space of consciousness (cidākāśa)

## Cross References

- Brahman
- Prana
- Agni
- Shabda (sound — the quality of akasha)
- Kosha

## Open Research Questions

- What is the relationship between the Vaiśeṣika concept of ākāśa as a substance and the modern concept of spacetime?
- How does the concept of cidākāśa (consciousness-space) relate to modern theories of consciousness?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some physicists propose that the quantum vacuum (the ground state of quantum field theory) has structural similarities to the Vedic concept of ākāśa as the luminous ground of all existence. This remains a philosophical analogy.

## Canonical Sources

- Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1 (ākāśa as the first element)
- Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1 (Brahman as ākāśa)
- Vaiśeṣika Sūtras 2.1.27 (ākāśa as a substance)
- Bhagavad Gītā 9.6 (all beings exist in ākāśa like the wind in space)

# Yantra

## Canonical Name

Yantra

## Sanskrit

यन्त्र

## Transliteration

Yantra

## Śabda

यन्त्र

## Dhātu

यम् (Yam) — To restrain, to hold, to support, to govern.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from the verbal root यम् (yam) with the suffix -tra (instrument suffix). Neuter noun. Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.2.182 governs the -tra suffix. Yantra = that which restrains, holds, or governs; an instrument of control and support.

## Nirukta

"Yantrayati iti yantraḥ" — that which restrains or governs. The root yam carries the sense of holding in place, governing, and directing. A yantra holds the divine presence in geometric form.

## Bīja

The bīja of the specific deity whose yantra is being used. For Śrī Yantra: hrīṃ (Māyā-śakti bīja). For Gaṇeśa Yantra: gaṃ. For Sūrya Yantra: hrāṃ. The central bindu (point) of every yantra is itself the supreme bīja.

## Tattva

Yantra-Tattva — the principle of geometric form as a vehicle of divine presence. In Tantric philosophy: the yantra is the geometric body of the deity, as the mantra is the sonic body and the mūrti (image) is the physical body. The yantra operates through the principle of correspondence between geometric form and cosmic structure.

## Śakti

Yantra-Śakti — the power concentrated in geometric form. The Śrī Yantra is considered the geometric form of Śakti herself. The nine interlocking triangles of the Śrī Yantra represent the nine forms of Śakti. The bindu at the center is the seat of Śakti's supreme power.

## Literal Meaning

Instrument; device; that which restrains or holds; a geometric diagram.

## Functional Meaning

Yantra is a geometric diagram used as a support for meditation, worship, and the concentration of divine energy. It is the visual counterpart of mantra — as mantra is the sonic form of the deity, yantra is the geometric form. The yantra operates through the principle that specific geometric configurations correspond to specific states of consciousness and cosmic forces. The practitioner meditates on the yantra, moving from the outer geometric forms inward to the central bindu, which represents the undifferentiated source.

## Ontology

In Tantric philosophy: the yantra is not merely a symbol but a living geometric body of the deity. The Śrī Yantra is the geometric form of the entire cosmos as Śakti's body. In Advaita: the yantra is an upāsanā (contemplative) support that leads the mind from form to formlessness. In Śākta tradition: the yantra is the primary form of the Goddess — more fundamental than the anthropomorphic image.

## Cosmology

The Śrī Yantra represents the entire cosmos: the nine interlocking triangles represent the nine levels of manifestation. The outer square represents the earth plane. The lotus petals represent the unfolding of creation. The central bindu represents the undifferentiated source. The yantra is a map of the cosmos and a map of consciousness simultaneously.

## Psychology

The yantra functions as a visual mantra — sustained meditation on the yantra produces the same psychological transformation as mantra recitation. The geometric progression from outer to inner mirrors the psychological journey from gross to subtle consciousness. The central bindu represents the state of pure awareness beyond all form.

## Governance

In Vedic governance: yantras were used in the consecration of temples, cities, and royal palaces. The concept of vāstu-yantra (architectural yantra) governs the geometric layout of sacred spaces. The Arthaśāstra describes the use of protective yantras in statecraft.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: yantras are used as protective amulets (rakṣā-yantra) and healing supports. Specific yantras are prescribed for specific conditions. The Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Yantra is used for healing and protection.

## Mathematics

The Śrī Yantra is a mathematical marvel: the nine interlocking triangles create 43 smaller triangles with precise geometric relationships. The angles and proportions of the Śrī Yantra follow specific mathematical rules. The concept of sacred geometry (yantra-gaṇita) is a distinct mathematical tradition.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: each of the nine planets (navagraha) has a corresponding yantra. Planetary yantras are used during specific astronomical configurations. The Navagraha Yantra maps the nine planets in a geometric arrangement.

## Metallurgy

Yantras are traditionally inscribed on metal plates (copper, gold, silver) or stone. The choice of metal corresponds to the deity: gold for solar deities, silver for lunar deities, copper for Śakti. The process of yantra inscription involves specific mantras and ritual procedures.

## Ritual

The yantra is the primary ritual support in Tantric worship (pūjā). The ritual of yantra-prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā (consecration of the yantra) installs the deity's presence in the geometric form. The Navāvaraṇa pūjā (nine-enclosure worship) of the Śrī Yantra is the most elaborate Tantric ritual.

## Symbolism

The triangle pointing upward (trikona) represents Śiva/masculine principle. The triangle pointing downward represents Śakti/feminine principle. The interlocking triangles represent the union of Śiva and Śakti. The lotus represents purity and unfolding. The square represents the earth and the four directions. The bindu represents the undifferentiated source.

## Related Deities

- Devī/Tripurasundarī (the Śrī Yantra is her geometric body)
- Gaṇeśa (Gaṇeśa Yantra)
- Sūrya (Sūrya Yantra)
- Śiva (Śiva Yantra)
- Viṣṇu (Viṣṇu Yantra)

## Related Lokas

- All lokas are represented within the Śrī Yantra's geometric structure
- The nine enclosures of the Śrī Yantra correspond to nine levels of cosmic manifestation

## Related Koshas

- All five koshas are represented in the Śrī Yantra's structure
- The central bindu corresponds to the Ānandamaya Kosha (bliss sheath)

## Related Chakras

- The Śrī Yantra corresponds to the Sahasrāra (crown chakra)
- Each chakra has a corresponding yantra (the chakra itself is a yantra)
- Mūlādhāra: square yantra; Svādhiṣṭhāna: crescent yantra; Maṇipūra: triangle yantra

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (the supreme yantra of Śakti)
- Gaṇeśa Yantra
- Navagraha Yantra
- Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Yantra
- Kuber Yantra

## Related Mantras

- Śrī Vidyā mantra (the mantra corresponding to the Śrī Yantra)
- Gāyatrī Mantra (corresponding to the Gāyatrī Yantra)
- Navagraha mantras (corresponding to the Navagraha Yantra)

## Related Vidyās

- Yantra-Vidyā (the science of sacred geometry)
- Tantra-Vidyā (the science of Śakti worship)
- Vāstu-Vidyā (the science of sacred architecture)

## Related Śāstras

- Tantrasāra (Abhinavagupta) — yantra in Kashmir Śaivism
- Śāradātilaka Tantra — yantra construction and use
- Devī Māhātmya — the Goddess's geometric forms
- Mantra-Mahodadhi — systematic treatment of yantras and mantras

## Traditional Interpretations

- Śākta: The yantra is the primary form of the Goddess — more fundamental than the anthropomorphic image; the Śrī Yantra is the Goddess herself
- Kashmir Śaivism: The yantra is the geometric form of Śiva's consciousness; meditation on the yantra is meditation on consciousness itself
- Advaita: The yantra is an upāsanā support that leads the mind from form to formlessness
- Vaiṣṇava: Yantras are used in temple worship as geometric supports for deity presence
- Smārta: Yantras are used in the pañcāyatana (five-deity) worship system

## Historical Evolution

- Vedic period: Geometric altars (vedi) in Śulbasūtras are proto-yantras
- Upaniṣadic period: The concept of the body as yantra (the body as the deity's geometric form)
- Tantric period (500–1200 CE): Yantras systematized; the Śrī Yantra reaches its classical form
- Medieval: Yantra traditions codified in Āgamas and Tantras
- Modern: Yantras used in meditation and as sacred art

## Cross References

- Mantra
- Tantra
- Shakti
- Chakras
- Prana
- Om

## Open Research Questions

- What is the mathematical relationship between the Śrī Yantra's geometry and the structure of consciousness?
- How do the different yantra traditions (Śākta, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava) relate to each other?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some researchers propose that the geometric forms of yantras correspond to specific patterns of neural activity during meditation. This remains under scientific investigation and is not established in any canonical tradition.

## Canonical Sources

- Tantrasāra (Abhinavagupta) — yantra in Kashmir Śaivism
- Śāradātilaka Tantra — yantra construction
- Devī Māhātmya (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa) — the Goddess's geometric forms
- Baudhāyana Śulbasūtra — geometric altar construction (proto-yantra)

# Karma

## Canonical Name

Karma

## Sanskrit

कर्म

## Transliteration

Karma

## Śabda

कर्म

## Dhātu

कृ (Kṛ) — To do, perform, act, make.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from the verbal root कृ (kṛ) with the suffix -man (neuter noun). Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.3.18. Karma is a neuter noun meaning "action" or "deed." In grammar, karma also denotes the object of a verb (karman = object/patient).

## Nirukta

Yāska: "kriyate anena iti karma" — that by which action is performed. The root kṛ encompasses all forms of doing, making, and performing.

## Bīja

क (Ka) — the seed syllable of action and creation in Tantric traditions. Associated with Brahmā (the creator) whose bīja is also Ka.

## Tattva

Karma-Tattva — the principle of causation through action. In Sāṃkhya: karma is the activity of the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas). In Vaiśeṣika: karma is one of the seven padārthas (categories), defined as motion. In Vedānta: karma is the mechanism of saṃsāra (cycle of rebirth).

## Śakti

Kriyā-Śakti — the power of action. One of the three fundamental śaktis (icchā-jñāna-kriyā). Karma operates through kriyā-śakti as the dynamic force of manifestation.

## Literal Meaning

Action; deed; work; ritual act.

## Functional Meaning

Karma is the universal principle that every action generates corresponding consequences. It operates across three dimensions: Sañcita karma (accumulated past actions), Prārabdha karma (karma currently bearing fruit), and Āgāmi/Kriyamāṇa karma (karma being created now). The law of karma is not punishment but the natural law of cause and effect operating through consciousness.

## Ontology

In Mīmāṃsā: karma (ritual action) is the primary means of achieving dharmic results; the apūrva (unseen potency) of ritual karma persists until it bears fruit. In Advaita Vedānta: karma operates only at the vyāvahārika level; from the absolute standpoint, there is no doer, hence no karma. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: karma is real and must be exhausted through bhakti and surrender to Viṣṇu. In Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika: karma is one of seven categories of reality, defined as motion (pariṇāma).

## Cosmology

Karma drives the cycle of saṃsāra across all fourteen lokas. The Purāṇas describe karma as the mechanism by which souls transmigrate through different realms. In Jain cosmology, karma is a subtle material substance (karma-pudgala) that adheres to the soul (jīva) and determines its condition. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa describes karma as the force that maintains the cosmic order of creation, preservation, and dissolution.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology: karma creates saṃskāras (mental impressions) and vāsanās (latent tendencies) that condition future experience. Patañjali's Yoga Sūtras 2.12-14 describe the karma-āśaya (karma-store) as the root of birth, lifespan, and experience. Karma operates through the kāraṇa-śarīra (causal body). Karma yoga (the yoga of action) transforms karma from bondage to liberation by eliminating the sense of doership (ahaṃkāra).

## Marathi Summary

कर्मयोग म्हणजे आपले कर्तव्यकर्म करणे, पण त्याच्या फळाची आसक्ती न ठेवणे. अशा कृतीतून अहंभाव कमी होतो आणि कर्मबंधनातून मुक्त होण्याचा मार्ग मिळतो.

## Governance

Karma as social principle: the concept of karma-phala (fruit of action) underlies Indian jurisprudence. Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra recognizes that rulers accumulate karma through their governance. The concept of rāja-dharma (royal duty) is the karmic responsibility of the king. Historical Indian governance was explicitly framed in karmic terms — Aśoka's dhamma edicts reflect karmic accountability.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: karma is one of the causes of disease (prājñāparādha — crime against wisdom is a karmic cause). Caraka Saṃhitā identifies karma as a factor in the etiology of disease. Karmic diseases (ādhidaivika) require spiritual remedies alongside physical treatment. The concept of karma-ja-vyādhi (karma-born disease) is a distinct category in Āyurvedic pathology.

## Mathematics

The mathematical principle of karma is the law of conservation: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Vedic mathematics (Gaṇita) treats karma as the principle of balance — equations must balance, debts must be settled. The concept of ṛṇa (debt) in Vedic mathematics mirrors the karmic debt concept.

## Astronomy

Karma in Jyotiṣa (Vedic astrology): the birth chart (janma-kuṇḍali) is considered a map of prārabdha karma. Planetary positions at birth reflect accumulated karma. The concept of daśā (planetary period) describes the timing of karmic fruition. Graha (planets) are considered agents of karma delivery.

## Metallurgy

In Viśvakarmā tradition: the karma of the craftsman (śilpin) determines the quality of the work. The concept of karma-yoga in craft: the craftsman who works without attachment to results produces the finest work. The dharma of metals (their inherent properties) must be respected — working against a metal's karma produces inferior results.

## Ritual

Karma-kāṇḍa (ritual section of the Vedas) is the primary domain of Mīmāṃsā. The sixteen saṃskāras are karmic rituals that shape the individual's karmic trajectory. Yajña (sacrifice) is the highest karmic act — it purifies accumulated karma and generates positive karma. Prāyaścitta (expiation) rituals neutralize specific karmic debts.

## Symbolism

The wheel (cakra) symbolizes karma's cyclical nature. The scales represent karmic balance. The seed (bīja) represents karma's potential — every action is a seed that will bear fruit. The mirror represents karma's reflective nature — what you do returns to you. The knot (granthi) represents karmic bondage.

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Karma is ultimately unreal from the absolute standpoint; jñāna (knowledge) alone destroys karma
- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Karma is real and must be surrendered to Viṣṇu through prapatti (surrender)
- Dvaita (Madhva): Karma is eternally real; liberation requires Viṣṇu's grace to transcend karma
- Mīmāṃsā: Karma (ritual action) is the primary means of achieving all human goals
- Buddhism: Karma is intentional action (cetanā); it is the intention, not the act, that creates karma
- Jainism: Karma is a subtle material substance that binds the soul; liberation requires exhausting all karma through tapas (austerity)

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Karma primarily means ritual action; cosmic karma (ṛta) governs the universe
- Brāhmaṇa period: Karma as ritual action is elaborated extensively; karma-kāṇḍa develops
- Upaniṣadic period: Karma as ethical-spiritual principle emerges; karma-saṃsāra connection established
- Buddhist period (500 BCE): Karma redefined as intentional action; karma-rebirth doctrine systematized
- Jain period: Karma as material substance — unique and influential formulation
- Epic-Purāṇic period: Karma as cosmic justice mechanism; karma-yoga as path to liberation
- Medieval: Karma integrated into bhakti traditions — karma surrendered to God

# Rta

## Canonical Name

Rta

## Sanskrit

ऋत

## Transliteration

Ṛta

## Śabda

ऋत

## Dhātu

ऋ (Ṛ) — To go, to move, to flow. Ṛta is "that which has moved/flowed in the right way" — the right order of things.

## Vyākaraṇa

Ṛta is a neuter noun derived from the past passive participle of the root ṛ (to go/flow). It means "that which has gone rightly" — the right order, the truth, the cosmic law.

## Nirukta

Yāska: "ṛtam — satyam" — Ṛta is truth. The cosmic truth that underlies all existence. Ṛta is both the cosmic order and the truth that expresses it.

## Bīja

ऋ (Ṛ) — the vowel ṛ itself is the bīja of cosmic order and right movement.

## Tattva

Ṛta-Tattva — the principle of cosmic truth and right order. Ṛta is the Vedic precursor to Dharma — the cosmic law that governs all existence before it was articulated as ethical principle.

## Śakti

Ṛta-Śakti — the power of cosmic truth. The śakti that maintains the right order of the universe — the movements of the sun, the seasons, the moral order of human society.

## Literal Meaning

Cosmic order; truth; right; the law of the universe.

## Functional Meaning

Ṛta is the Vedic concept of cosmic truth and right order. It governs the movements of the celestial bodies, the cycle of seasons, the moral order of human society, and the efficacy of ritual. Varuṇa is the primary guardian of Ṛta — he punishes those who violate it. Ṛta is the foundation from which Dharma (ethical order) later developed. The concept of Ṛta underlies the Vedic understanding of truth (satya) — to speak truth is to align with Ṛta.

## Ontology

In Vedic ontology: Ṛta is the cosmic law that precedes and underlies all existence. It is not created by the gods but is the principle by which the gods themselves operate. In later philosophy: Ṛta becomes Dharma (ethical order) and Satya (truth) — the two primary expressions of cosmic law.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: Ṛta governs the movements of the sun (Sūrya follows Ṛta), the cycle of seasons (ṛtu — season — derives from Ṛta), the flow of rivers, and the moral order of the universe. The concept of Ṛta-dhāman (the abode of Ṛta) — the cosmic realm where Ṛta is perfectly expressed.

## Psychology

Ṛta as psychological principle: the person who lives in alignment with Ṛta experiences inner harmony. The violation of Ṛta (anṛta — untruth, adharma) creates psychological disturbance. The concept of ṛta-cit (Ṛta-consciousness) — the mind that perceives and aligns with cosmic truth.

## Governance

Ṛta as the foundation of governance: the king who governs according to Ṛta maintains cosmic order. The concept of rāja-dharma (royal duty) is the application of Ṛta to governance. Varuṇa's role as the guardian of Ṛta is the model for the king's role as the guardian of dharma.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Ṛta as the right order of the body — health is the body's alignment with Ṛta. The concept of ṛtu-caryā (seasonal regimen) — living according to the seasonal Ṛta for optimal health.

## Mathematics

The concept of Ṛta in mathematics: mathematical truth (satya) is a form of Ṛta — the right order of numbers and relationships. The Vedic concept of mathematical precision in ritual (Śulbasūtras) is an expression of Ṛta.

## Astronomy

Ṛta is most directly expressed in astronomy — the right movements of celestial bodies. The concept of ṛtu (season) derives from Ṛta — the seasons are the cosmic Ṛta expressed in time. Vedic astronomy (Jyotiṣa) is the science of tracking Ṛta in the sky.

## Metallurgy

The concept of Ṛta in metallurgy: the right order of metallurgical processes — following the dharma of each metal is following its Ṛta.

## Ritual

Yajña (sacrifice) is the primary ritual expression of Ṛta — it maintains and reinforces cosmic order. The concept of ṛta-yajña (sacrifice according to Ṛta) — ritual performed in alignment with cosmic truth. The Vedic concept of ṛtvij (the priest who performs the ritual at the right time — ṛtu + ij) — the priest who aligns ritual with Ṛta.

## Symbolism

The sun symbolizes Ṛta — it follows its ordained path without deviation. The river symbolizes Ṛta — it flows in its right course. The seasons symbolize Ṛta — they follow their right order.

## Related Deities

- Varuṇa (the primary guardian of Ṛta — he punishes violations of cosmic order)
- Mitra (Varuṇa's companion — together they uphold Ṛta)
- Sūrya (the sun — the most visible expression of Ṛta in the cosmos)
- Agni (the fire — the ritual medium of Ṛta)

## Related Lokas

- Ṛta-dhāman (the abode of Ṛta — the cosmic realm of perfect order)

## Related Koshas

## Related Chakras

# Ahimsa

## Canonical Name

Ahimsa

## Sanskrit

अहिंसा

## Transliteration

Ahimsa

## Literal Meaning

Non-violence; non-harm; non-injury. From Sanskrit a (not) + himsa (violence, harm, injury).

## Ahimsa Paramo Dharma

The phrase **Ahimsa Paramo Dharma** (अहिंसा परमो धर्मः) means:

**"Non-violence is the highest dharma."**

- Ahimsa = non-violence
- Paramo = highest, supreme
- Dharma = duty, righteousness, cosmic order

This maxim appears in the Mahabharata (Anushasana Parva 115.1) and is one of the most cited ethical statements in Indian tradition. The full verse continues: "Ahimsa paramo dharma, tatha ahimsa paramo tapah" — Non-violence is the highest dharma; non-violence is the highest austerity.

## Functional Meaning

Ahimsa is the principle of not causing harm to any living being — in thought, word, or action. It is the foundational ethical principle shared across Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist traditions. In Jainism, ahimsa is the first and supreme vow. In Yoga, ahimsa is the first of the five Yamas (ethical restraints) in Patanjali's Ashtanga Yoga. In the Mahabharata, ahimsa is declared the highest dharma.

## Marathi Summary

अहिंसा म्हणजे विचार, शब्द किंवा कृतीतून कोणत्याही सजीवाला इजा न करणे. जैन परंपरेत ती सर्वोच्च व्रत मानली जाते.

## Jain Teaching on Ahimsa

The Acharanga Sutra (the oldest Jain canonical text) states the core teaching of ahimsa:

"All beings desire to live. None wishes to die. Therefore, a wise person does not kill, nor causes others to kill, nor consents to killing."

The Five Great Vows (Mahavrata) for Jain monks place Ahimsa first:
1. Ahimsa — Non-violence toward all living beings
2. Satya — Absolute truthfulness
3. Asteya — Non-stealing
4. Brahmacharya — Celibacy
5. Aparigraha — Complete non-possessiveness

UniGuru Citation: Acharanga Sutra, Book 1, Lecture 7; Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22, Jacobi translation

## Yoga Teaching on Ahimsa

In Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (2.30), Ahimsa is the first of the five Yamas:
"Ahimsa-satya-asteya-brahmacharya-aparigraha yamah" — Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the five restraints.

Patanjali states (Yoga Sutras 2.35): "Ahimsa-pratishthayam tat-sannidhau vaira-tyagah" — When one is established in non-violence, all enmity is abandoned in one's presence.

## Dharma Connection

The Mahabharata (Anushasana Parva) states: "Ahimsa paramo dharma" — Non-violence is the highest dharma. The Caraka Samhita (Ayurvedic text) states that the physician's svadharma includes ahimsa (non-harm) as the first ethical principle. Dharma.md cross-references Ahimsa as a related concept.

## Cosmology and Ethics

Ahimsa operates at multiple levels:
- Physical: not harming the body of any being
- Verbal: not speaking words that harm
- Mental: not harboring harmful thoughts

In Jain cosmology, every act of violence (himsa) generates karma that binds the soul. Ahimsa is therefore both an ethical principle and a metaphysical necessity for liberation (moksha).

## Related Concepts

- Dharma (Ahimsa paramo dharma — non-violence is the highest dharma)
- Karma (violence generates binding karma)
- Moksha (ahimsa is necessary for liberation)
- Satya (truth — the second great vow, companion to ahimsa)
- Yoga (ahimsa is the first Yama in Patanjali's system)

## Related Shastras

- Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva (primary source for "Ahimsa paramo dharma")
- Acharanga Sutra (Jain canonical source — oldest text on ahimsa)
- Yoga Sutras of Patanjali (2.30 — ahimsa as first Yama)
- Caraka Samhita (Ayurvedic ethics — ahimsa as physician's duty)
- Tattvartha Sutra (Jain systematic philosophy of ahimsa)

# Dharma

## Canonical Name

Dharma

## Sanskrit

धर्म

## Transliteration

Dharma

## Śabda

धर्म

## Dhātu

धृ (Dhṛ) — To uphold, sustain, support.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from the verbal root धृ (dhṛ) with the suffix -man. Masculine noun, second declension. Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.3.18 governs the suffix formation.

## Nirukta

Yāska's Nirukta: "dharayati iti dharmaḥ" — that which upholds is Dharma. The root dhṛ carries the sense of bearing, sustaining, maintaining cosmic and social order.

## Bīja

ध (Dha) — the seed syllable associated with sustaining force in Tantric traditions.

## Tattva

Ṛta-Dharma Tattva — the principle of cosmic and moral order that sustains all existence. In Sāṃkhya: Dharma is a quality (guṇa) of the Mahat (cosmic intellect). In Vedānta: Dharma is the expression of Ṛta at the human level.

## Śakti

Dharma-Śakti — the preserving and ordering power. Associated with Viṣṇu's sustaining function (sthiti-śakti). In Śākta traditions, Dharma is upheld by the Goddess as Mahāmāyā maintaining cosmic law.

## Literal Meaning

That which is upheld; that which upholds. The sustaining principle.

## Functional Meaning

Dharma is the universal principle governing righteous conduct, cosmic order, social duty, and individual ethics. It operates simultaneously at four levels: Ṛta (cosmic order), Varṇāśrama-dharma (social order), Svadharma (individual duty), and Sādhāraṇa-dharma (universal ethics applicable to all beings).

## Marathi Summary

धर्म म्हणजे योग्य आचरण, सामाजिक कर्तव्य, वैश्विक व्यवस्था आणि सर्वांसाठी लागू होणारी नैतिकता टिकवून ठेवणारे तत्त्व.

## Ontology

In Vaiśeṣika: Dharma is a padārtha (category of reality) — the cause of abhyudaya (worldly prosperity) and niḥśreyasa (liberation). In Mīmāṃsā: Dharma is codanā-lakṣaṇa — that which is enjoined by Vedic injunction. In Advaita Vedānta: Dharma at the vyāvahārika (conventional) level is real and necessary; at the pāramārthika (absolute) level, only Brahman exists.

## Cosmology

Dharma is one of the four Puruṣārthas (aims of human life): Dharma, Artha, Kāma, Mokṣa. In the Purāṇic cosmology, Dharma is personified as a deity, son of Brahmā, husband of ten daughters of Dakṣa. In the four yugas (Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali), Dharma stands on four legs, three, two, and one respectively — indicating progressive decline of cosmic order.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology (Patañjali): Dharma-megha-samādhi is the highest samādhi, the "cloud of virtue" that rains liberation. Dharma as psychological principle governs the sattva-rajas-tamas balance in the individual. Right action (dharmic action) produces psychological clarity (citta-prasāda).

## Governance

Rājadharma (royal duty) is elaborated in Manusmṛti, Arthaśāstra, Mahābhārata Śāntiparva. The king's primary duty is dharma-rakṣaṇa (protection of dharma). Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra treats dharma as the foundation of statecraft. Aśoka's dhamma edicts represent the historical application of dharmic governance.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Dharma is the foundation of Āyurvedic ethics. The physician's svadharma includes ahiṃsā (non-harm), satya (truth), and service. Caraka Saṃhitā Sūtrasthāna 1.15 states that the physician who follows dharma achieves both worldly success and liberation.

## Mathematics

Dharma as cosmic order underlies the mathematical precision of Vedic ritual geometry (Śulbasūtras). The Pythagorean theorem appears in Baudhāyana Śulbasūtra as a dharmic requirement for altar construction. Mathematical truth (satya) is considered a form of dharma.

## Astronomy

Ṛta (cosmic order, precursor to dharma) governs the movements of celestial bodies. Vedic astronomy (Jyotiṣa) treats planetary motion as dharmic — planets follow their ordained paths. The concept of ṛtu (season) derives from ṛta, linking dharma to astronomical cycles.

## Metallurgy

In Viśvakarmā tradition: the dharma of metals is their inherent nature and proper use. Gold (suvarṇa) has the dharma of purity; iron (ayasa) has the dharma of strength. Proper metallurgical practice follows the dharma of each material.

## Ritual

Yajña (sacrifice) is the primary ritual expression of dharma. The Mīmāṃsā school holds that Vedic ritual injunctions (vidhi) define dharma. Dharma-śāstra prescribes the sixteen saṃskāras (life-cycle rituals) as the ritual framework of dharmic life. Sandhyāvandana (daily worship) is the minimal dharmic ritual obligation.

## Symbolism

Dharma is symbolized by the wheel (dharmacakra) — the Buddha's first teaching is the "turning of the wheel of dharma." The scales of justice represent dharma's balancing function. The lotus represents dharma's purity amid worldly existence. The cow (go) is the living symbol of dharma in Vedic tradition.

- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Dharma is bhakti-yoga — devotional service to Viṣṇu is the highest dharma
- Dvaita (Madhva): Dharma is the eternal will of Viṣṇu; individual dharma is participation in divine order

- Atharvaveda: Dharma begins to acquire social and ethical dimensions
- Upaniṣadic period: Dharma becomes internalized as ethical-spiritual principle
- Epic period (Mahābhārata): Dharma becomes the central problematic — the Gītā's entire teaching is dharmic

# Guru

## Canonical Name

Guru

## Sanskrit

गुरु

## Transliteration

Guru

## Śabda

गुरु

## Dhātu

गृ (Gṛ) — To swallow, to take in; also connected to गुर् (Gur) — heavy, weighty. The guru is the "heavy one" — weighty with knowledge.

## Vyākaraṇa

Guru is an adjective (meaning "heavy, weighty, important") used as a noun. It is also used as a title. The feminine form is Gurū or Gurviṇī. The word is used in both the sense of "teacher" and "heavy/important."

## Nirukta

"Gu-kāraś cāndhakārasya ru-kāras tannirodhakṛt" — Gu represents darkness (ignorance), Ru represents its removal. The Guru is one who removes the darkness of ignorance. This etymology appears in the Advayatāraka Upaniṣad.

## Bīja

गुं (Guṃ) — the bīja associated with the Guru principle in Tantric traditions.

## Tattva

Guru-Tattva — the principle of the teacher who transmits knowledge and removes ignorance. In Kashmir Śaivism: Guru-tattva is one of the thirty-six tattvas — the principle of divine grace operating through the human teacher.

## Śakti

Guru-Śakti — the power of the teacher to transmit knowledge and grace. The concept of śakti-pāta (descent of grace) — the Guru's transmission of spiritual power to the student.

## Literal Meaning

Heavy; weighty; important; teacher; spiritual master.

## Functional Meaning

The Guru is the teacher who transmits knowledge (vidyā) from the tradition to the student. In the Vedic tradition, knowledge cannot be obtained from books alone — it must be transmitted from Guru to student in an unbroken lineage (paramparā). The Guru removes the student's ignorance (avidyā) and guides them toward liberation (mokṣa). The Guru-śiṣya (teacher-student) relationship is the foundational relationship of Indian civilization.

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta: the Guru is the external manifestation of the inner Guru (Ātman). The Guru's teaching points the student to their own true nature. In Tantra: the Guru is the living embodiment of the divine — "Guru is Brahma, Guru is Viṣṇu, Guru is Maheśvara" (Guru Gītā). In Kashmir Śaivism: the Guru is the agent of Śiva's grace — śakti-pāta operates through the Guru.

## Cosmology

In Purāṇic cosmology: Bṛhaspati is the Guru of the gods (deva-guru); Śukra is the Guru of the demons (asura-guru). The concept of Ādi-Guru (the first Guru) — Śiva is the Ādi-Guru who taught yoga to Pārvatī. The concept of Guru-paramparā (lineage of teachers) — the unbroken chain from the divine source to the present teacher.

## Psychology

The Guru-śiṣya relationship as psychological transformation: the Guru mirrors the student's unconscious patterns and guides their dissolution. The concept of guru-bhakti (devotion to the Guru) as a psychological practice — surrendering the ego to the Guru's guidance. The concept of guru-kṛpā (Guru's grace) — the transformative power of the Guru's attention and blessing.

## Governance

The concept of Guru in governance: the rāja-guru (royal teacher) was the king's spiritual and political advisor. Cāṇakya (Kauṭilya) was the paradigmatic rāja-guru — he guided Candragupta Maurya to establish the Maurya Empire. The concept of dharma-guru (teacher of righteousness) — the Guru who guides the ruler in dharmic governance.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: the Guru is the teacher of medical knowledge. The Guru-śiṣya relationship is the primary mode of Āyurvedic transmission. The concept of guru-upadeśa (Guru's instruction) as the most important element of Āyurvedic education. The Guru's direct observation and correction of the student's practice is essential.

## Mathematics

The concept of Guru in mathematics: the transmission of mathematical knowledge through the Guru-śiṣya relationship. The Āryabhaṭīya and other mathematical texts were transmitted through Guru-paramparā. The concept of guru-mukha-vidyā (knowledge from the Guru's mouth) — mathematical knowledge that cannot be obtained from texts alone.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Guru (Jupiter) is the planet of wisdom, teaching, and expansion. Jupiter is the Guru of the solar system — the largest planet, the teacher of the other planets. The concept of guru-bala (Jupiter's strength) in the birth chart — a strong Jupiter indicates wisdom and good teachers.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: the Guru is the master alchemist who transmits the secret knowledge of Rasaśāstra. The concept of guru-dīkṣā (initiation by the Guru) in alchemy — the student cannot practice alchemy without the Guru's initiation and guidance.

## Ritual

The Guru-pūjā (worship of the Guru) is performed on Guru Pūrṇimā (the full moon of Āṣāḍha). The Guru-vandanā (salutation to the Guru) begins all learning. The concept of guru-dakṣiṇā (gift to the Guru) — the student's offering to the Guru upon completion of study. The Upanayana saṃskāra initiates the student into the Guru-śiṣya relationship.

## Symbolism

The lamp (dīpa) symbolizes the Guru — the Guru's knowledge illuminates the student's darkness. The sun symbolizes the Guru — the source of light and life. The river symbolizes the Guru's teaching — it flows from the source (tradition) to nourish the student.

## Related Deities

- Bṛhaspati (the Guru of the gods — the divine teacher)
- Dattātreya (the Guru of all gurus — the avadhūta teacher)
- Śiva (Ādi-Guru — the first teacher of yoga)
- Sarasvatī (the Goddess of learning — the divine Guru)
- Gaṇeśa (the remover of obstacles in learning)

## Related Lokas

- Guru-loka (the realm of the teacher — Jupiter's realm)

- Sahasrāra (crown chakra) — the seat of the Guru's grace (guru-pīṭha)

- Bṛhaspati Yantra (for Jupiter's wisdom)

# Brahman

## Canonical Name

Brahman

## Sanskrit

ब्रह्मन्

## Transliteration

Brahman

## Śabda

ब्रह्मन्

## Dhātu

बृह् (Bṛh) — To expand, to grow, to be great.

## Vyākaraṇa

Brahman is a neuter noun (not to be confused with Brahmā, the masculine creator deity, or Brāhmaṇa, the priestly class). Derived from the root bṛh with the suffix -man. The neuter gender indicates that Brahman transcends all categories including gender.

## Nirukta

Yāska: "bṛhati iti brahma" — that which is great, that which expands. Brahman is the infinitely expanding reality that underlies all existence.

## Bīja

ॐ (Om/Auṃ) — the primordial sound that is the sonic form of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad opens: "Auṃ ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvam" — Om, this syllable is all this.

## Tattva

Brahma-Tattva — the principle of absolute, infinite, self-luminous reality. Brahman is described as Sat-Cit-Ānanda (Being-Consciousness-Bliss) — not three qualities but three aspects of one indivisible reality.

## Śakti

Brahman's śakti is Māyā — the creative power that projects the apparent multiplicity of the universe. In Śākta traditions, Brahman without Śakti is inert (śava); Brahman with Śakti is Śiva (the living absolute).

## Literal Meaning

The Absolute; the Infinite; the Ultimate Reality; the Ground of Being.

## Functional Meaning

Brahman is the infinite, eternal, unchanging absolute reality that is the ground of all existence. It is both the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) and the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) of the universe. Brahman is described via two approaches: Nirguṇa Brahman (without attributes — the absolute beyond all description) and Saguṇa Brahman (with attributes — the personal God, Īśvara). The Upaniṣads teach that Brahman is identical with Ātman (the individual Self).

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Brahman alone is real (Brahma satyam); the world is appearance (jagat mithyā); the individual self is Brahman (jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ). In Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Brahman is real, personal (Viṣṇu), and the universe and souls are Brahman's body. In Dvaita (Madhva): Brahman (Viṣṇu) is real and eternally distinct from souls and world. In Śaiva Siddhānta: Brahman is Śiva, the supreme reality with infinite śaktis.

## Cosmology

Brahman is the source, sustainer, and dissolution point of all universes. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante" — from which all beings are born, by which they live, into which they return — that is Brahman. The Purāṇas describe Brahman as the ocean from which the universe arises like waves. The concept of Brahmaṇḍa (Brahman's egg) is the cosmic egg from which the universe hatches.

## Psychology

Brahman as psychological reality: the deepest layer of consciousness is Brahman. In Yoga psychology, the state of samādhi (absorption) is the direct experience of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad identifies Brahman with the fourth state of consciousness (turīya) that underlies waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. The experience of Brahman is described as "neti neti" (not this, not this) — Brahman cannot be grasped by the mind but is the ground of the mind.

## Governance

The concept of Brahman in governance: the ideal ruler is one who has realized Brahman and governs from that realization. The Arthaśāstra's concept of the philosopher-king parallels the Upaniṣadic ideal of the Brahman-realized ruler. The concept of Brahma-rāṣṭra (the kingdom of Brahman) appears in Vedic literature as the ideal polity.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Brahman is the ultimate source of health (ārogya). The concept of Brahma-cakra (the cycle of Brahman) underlies the Āyurvedic understanding of the body as a microcosm of the universe. The highest healing is Brahma-jñāna (knowledge of Brahman) which removes the root cause of all disease — avidyā (ignorance).

## Mathematics

The concept of Brahman in mathematics: Brahman as the infinite (ananta) is the philosophical basis for the Indian mathematical concept of infinity. The concept of śūnya (zero) as the void from which all numbers emerge mirrors the Brahman-as-source concept. The Upaniṣadic statement "pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam" (that is full, this is full) is a mathematical statement about the nature of infinity.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Brahman is identified with the cosmic space (ākāśa) in which all celestial bodies move. The concept of Brahma-muhūrta (the hour of Brahman — 1.5 hours before sunrise) is the most auspicious time for spiritual practice. The Milky Way (Ākāśagaṅgā) is considered the visible form of Brahman's cosmic body.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: Brahman is the philosophical gold (parama-suvarṇa) — the ultimate substance that all metals aspire to become. The alchemical process of transmutation mirrors the spiritual process of realizing Brahman beneath the apparent multiplicity of substances.

## Ritual

The Brahma-yajña (sacrifice to Brahman) is the daily recitation of the Vedas — the highest ritual act. The Upanayana ceremony initiates the student into the study of Brahman. The Mahāvākyas are transmitted in ritual contexts as the direct teaching of Brahman. The concept of Brahma-vidyā (knowledge of Brahman) is the ultimate goal of all Vedic ritual.

## Symbolism

Om (ॐ) is the primary symbol of Brahman — the sound of the universe. The infinite space (ākāśa) symbolizes Brahman's all-pervading nature. The ocean symbolizes Brahman — waves (individual beings) arise from and return to the ocean. The sun symbolizes Nirguṇa Brahman — self-luminous, the source of all light. The bindu (point) in the center of a yantra represents Brahman as the source of all manifestation.

## Related Deities

- Brahman is not a deity but the ground of all deities
- Brahma (the creator) is Saguṇa Brahman's creative aspect
- Viṣṇu (the preserver) is Saguṇa Brahman's sustaining aspect
- Śiva (the destroyer) is Saguṇa Brahman's dissolving aspect
- Devī (the Goddess) is Brahman's Śakti — the dynamic aspect of the absolute

## Related Lokas

- Brahmaloka (Satyaloka) — the highest realm, closest to Brahman
- All lokas are within Brahman — "sarvam khalv idaṃ brahma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1)

## Related Koshas

- All five koshas are within Brahman
- Ānandamaya Kosha (bliss sheath) is the closest approximation to Brahman in the individual
- Beyond all koshas is Ātman = Brahman

## Related Chakras

- Sahasrāra (crown chakra) — the seat of Brahman realization in the individual body
- The entire chakra system is within Brahman

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (the geometric representation of Brahman's creative expansion)
- Bindu (the central point — Brahman as the source)

## Related Mantras

- "Aum" (the sonic form of Brahman)
- "Aham Brahmāsmi" (I am Brahman — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10)
- "Prajñānam Brahma" (Consciousness is Brahman — Aitareya Upaniṣad 3.3)
- "Sarvam khalv idaṃ brahma" (All this is indeed Brahman — Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1)

## Related Vidyās

- Brahmavidyā (knowledge of Brahman — the supreme vidyā)
- Ātmavidyā (self-knowledge = Brahmavidyā)
- Upaniṣad Vidyā (the teaching of the Upaniṣads)

## Related Śāstras

- Upaniṣads (primary source — especially Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Chāndogya, Taittirīya, Māṇḍūkya)
- Brahma Sūtras (Bādarāyaṇa — systematic exposition of Brahman)
- Bhagavad Gītā (Chapter 13 — Kṣetra-Kṣetrajña; Chapter 14 — Guṇatraya Vibhāga)
- Vivekacūḍāmaṇi (Śaṅkara)
- Brahma-Sūtra-Bhāṣya (Śaṅkara's commentary)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Brahman alone is real; world and individual self are appearances in Brahman
- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Brahman is personal (Viṣṇu); world and souls are Brahman's body
- Dvaita (Madhva): Brahman (Viṣṇu) is real and eternally distinct from souls and world
- Śaiva Siddhānta: Brahman is Śiva with infinite śaktis
- Śākta: Brahman is the Goddess (Devī) — the dynamic absolute
- Kashmir Śaivism: Brahman is Śiva-Śakti — pure consciousness and its creative power

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Brahman primarily means "sacred utterance" or "prayer power"
- Atharvaveda: Brahman as cosmic power
- Brāhmaṇa period: Brahman as the power of ritual
- Early Upaniṣads: Brahman as the ultimate reality, identical with Ātman
- Brahma Sūtras (200 BCE–200 CE): Systematic philosophy of Brahman
- Śaṅkara (8th century CE): Advaita — Brahman as the only reality
- Rāmānuja (11th century CE): Viśiṣṭādvaita — Brahman as personal God
- Madhva (13th century CE): Dvaita — Brahman as Viṣṇu, eternally distinct

- Moksha
- Maya

- Om

- Is Nirguṇa Brahman (attributeless absolute) a coherent philosophical concept, or does it collapse into nothingness?
- How does the Advaita concept of Brahman relate to the Buddhist concept of śūnyatā (emptiness)?
- What is the relationship between Brahman and the modern cosmological concept of the quantum vacuum?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some physicists and philosophers propose that the quantum vacuum (the ground state of quantum field theory) has structural similarities to the Upaniṣadic concept of Brahman as the ground of all existence. This remains a philosophical analogy, not an established scientific or canonical claim.

# Yoga

## Canonical Name

Yoga

## Sanskrit

योग

## Transliteration

Yoga

## Śabda

योग

## Dhātu

युज् (Yuj) — To yoke, to unite, to join, to concentrate.

## Vyākaraṇa

Yoga is a masculine noun derived from the root yuj with the suffix -a. The root yuj has two meanings: (1) yujir yoge — to unite; (2) yuj samādhau — to concentrate. Both meanings are operative in the concept of yoga.

## Nirukta

"Yujyate anena iti yogaḥ" — that by which union is achieved. Also: "yoge yukto bhavet" — one who is yoked (disciplined) is in yoga.

## Bīja

यं (Yaṃ) — the bīja of the air element (vāyu), associated with the heart chakra (Anāhata) and the breath-based practices of yoga.

## Tattva

Yoga-Tattva — the principle of union and integration. Yoga operates at multiple levels: union of individual self with universal Self (Advaita), union of Puruṣa with Prakṛti's dissolution (Sāṃkhya-Yoga), union of devotee with God (Bhakti-Yoga), union of action with non-attachment (Karma-Yoga).

## Śakti

Yoga-Śakti — the integrating power. The kuṇḍalinī-śakti is the primary yogic power that, when awakened, unites the individual with the universal. Prāṇa-śakti (life-force) is the medium through which yoga operates.

## Literal Meaning

Union; yoking; discipline; method; path.

## Functional Meaning

Yoga is the discipline leading to union of the individual self with the highest reality. Patañjali defines yoga as "yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ" — yoga is the cessation of the modifications of the mind-stuff. The Bhagavad Gītā defines yoga as "samatvam yoga ucyate" — equanimity is called yoga, and "yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam" — yoga is skill in action. The four classical paths are: Jñāna-Yoga (knowledge), Bhakti-Yoga (devotion), Karma-Yoga (action), Rāja-Yoga (meditation).

## Ontology

In Sāṃkhya-Yoga: yoga is the practical discipline that achieves the Sāṃkhya goal of Puruṣa's liberation from Prakṛti. In Advaita Vedānta: yoga is a means (sādhana) to the recognition of Ātman = Brahman. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: Bhakti-Yoga is the highest yoga — devotional union with Viṣṇu. In Tantra: yoga is the union of Śiva and Śakti within the practitioner's body.

## Cosmology

In Purāṇic cosmology: yoga is the cosmic principle of integration that holds the universe together. The concept of Yoga-Māyā (Viṣṇu's creative yoga-power) describes the divine yoga that maintains cosmic order. The Purāṇas describe Viṣṇu as eternally in yoga (yoga-nidrā — the yogic sleep of Viṣṇu).

## Psychology

Patañjali's Yoga Sūtras provide the most systematic psychology of yoga. The eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga): Yama (restraints), Niyama (observances), Āsana (posture), Prāṇāyāma (breath control), Pratyāhāra (sense withdrawal), Dhāraṇā (concentration), Dhyāna (meditation), Samādhi (absorption). The psychology of yoga maps the transformation of consciousness from ordinary awareness to liberation. The concept of citta (mind-stuff) and its five states (kṣipta, mūḍha, vikṣipta, ekāgra, niruddha) describes the psychological journey of yoga.

## Governance

The concept of yoga in governance: the Arthaśāstra recommends yogic practices for the ruler's mental clarity and decision-making. The concept of rāja-yoga (royal yoga) is both a spiritual path and a metaphor for the disciplined governance of the kingdom of the self. Aśoka's dhamma practice was essentially a form of governance-yoga.

## Medicine

Yoga as medicine: the Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā describes yoga as the cure for all diseases. Modern research confirms yoga's efficacy for stress, cardiovascular disease, mental health, and chronic pain. In Āyurveda: yoga is one of the three pillars of health alongside āhāra (diet) and vihāra (lifestyle). The concept of yoga-cikitsā (yoga therapy) is a distinct branch of Āyurvedic medicine.

## Mathematics

The concept of yoga in mathematics: the Vedic mathematical concept of "yoga" (addition/union) mirrors the spiritual concept. The Sulbasūtras use geometric yoga (union of areas) to construct ritual altars. The concept of saṃyoga (conjunction) in Vaiśeṣika philosophy is the mathematical-ontological basis of yoga.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: yoga refers to specific planetary combinations (graha-yoga) that indicate particular life patterns. There are 27 yogas in the Vedic calendar (based on the combined longitude of Sun and Moon). The concept of yoga in Jyotiṣa is directly derived from the root meaning of "union" — the union of planetary influences.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: yoga is the process of combining (yojana) substances to create new compounds. The Rasaśāstra tradition uses the concept of yoga (combination) as the basis of alchemical practice. The yoga of mercury (pārada) with sulfur (gandhaka) is the foundational alchemical yoga.

## Ritual

The Yoga-Sūtra's concept of Īśvara-praṇidhāna (surrender to God) is the ritual dimension of yoga. The concept of pūjā (worship) as yoga: the Bhagavad Gītā describes devotional worship as Bhakti-Yoga. The Tantric ritual of nyāsa (placing mantras on the body) is a form of yoga that unites the practitioner with the deity.

## Symbolism

The yoke (yoga) symbolizes the disciplined harnessing of the mind. The lotus in meditation posture symbolizes yoga — rooted in the earth, blooming toward the sky. The intertwined serpents (kuṇḍalinī) symbolize the yogic energy. The bindu (point of concentration) symbolizes the goal of yoga — one-pointed awareness.

# Kala

## Canonical Name

Kala

## Sanskrit

काल

## Transliteration

Kāla

## Śabda

काल

## Dhātu

कल् (Kal) — To count, to calculate; also connected to कल् (Kal) — to drive, to impel. Time is that which counts/measures and that which drives all things forward.

## Vyākaraṇa

Kāla is a masculine noun. It has two distinct meanings: (1) time (the cosmic principle), (2) death/Yama (the lord of time). The same word means both "time" and "death" — time is the force that leads all things to death.

## Nirukta

"Kalayati iti kālaḥ" — that which counts/measures. Also: "kālayati sarvam iti kālaḥ" — that which drives everything forward. Time is the universal driver.

## Bīja

क्रीं (Krīm) — the bīja of Kālī (the Goddess of time and death). Also कं (Kaṃ) — the bīja of Brahmā (the creator who operates within time).

## Tattva

Kāla-Tattva — the principle of time. In Sāṃkhya: Kāla is not a separate tattva but the mode of Prakṛti's activity. In Kashmir Śaivism: Kāla is one of the five kañcukas (coverings) that limit the universal consciousness — it limits the soul's experience to a particular time.

## Śakti

Kāla-Śakti — the power of time. The śakti that drives all change and transformation. Kālī (the Goddess of time) is the personification of Kāla-Śakti.

## Literal Meaning

Time; the right time; death; the black one (Kāla = black = death).

## Functional Meaning

Kāla is the universal principle of time that governs all change, growth, decay, and death. It operates at multiple levels: Kṣaṇa (moment), Muhūrta (48 minutes), Ahorātra (day-night), Pakṣa (fortnight), Māsa (month), Ṛtu (season), Ayana (half-year), Saṃvatsara (year), Yuga (cosmic age), Kalpa (cosmic cycle). The Bhagavad Gītā (11.32) identifies Kāla with Kṛṣṇa himself: "Kālo'smi loka-kṣaya-kṛt pravṛddhaḥ" — I am time, the destroyer of worlds.

## Ontology

In Vaiśeṣika: Kāla is one of the nine dravyas (substances) — eternal, all-pervading, the cause of all temporal relations. In Sāṃkhya: Kāla is not a separate substance but the mode of Prakṛti's activity. In Advaita: Kāla is within māyā — from the absolute standpoint, there is no time. In Kashmir Śaivism: Kāla is one of the five kañcukas that limit the soul.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: the four yugas (Kṛta/Satya, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali) constitute a mahāyuga (4,320,000 years). 1000 mahāyugas = one kalpa (day of Brahmā = 4.32 billion years). The concept of mahāpralaya (great dissolution) at the end of Brahmā's life (311 trillion years). The Purāṇas describe Kāla as the cosmic force that drives the universe through its cycles.

## Psychology

Kāla as psychological principle: the experience of time is subjective — time flies in joy and drags in suffering. The concept of kāla-jñāna (knowledge of time) — the wise person knows the right time for action. The concept of kāla-yoga (the yoga of time) — acting in alignment with the cosmic time.

## Governance

The concept of Kāla in governance: the Arthaśāstra emphasizes kāla (timing) as one of the most important factors in governance. The concept of kāla-nīti (time-policy) — the right action at the right time. The concept of kāla-cakra (wheel of time) in political philosophy — empires rise and fall according to the wheel of time.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Kāla (time) is one of the three causes of disease (along with karma and prajñāparādha). The concept of kāla-parīkṣā (examination of time) — the physician must consider the time of day, season, and stage of life in diagnosis and treatment. The concept of kāla-bala (strength of time) — certain times are more favorable for treatment.

## Mathematics

In Vedic mathematics: Kāla is the basis of the Indian number system — the large numbers (millions, billions, trillions) were developed to measure cosmic time. The concept of kāla-gaṇita (time calculation) — the mathematics of astronomical cycles.

## Astronomy

Jyotiṣa (Vedic astronomy) is fundamentally the science of Kāla — tracking the movements of celestial bodies to determine auspicious times. The concept of kāla-cakra (wheel of time) in Jyotiṣa — the zodiac as the wheel of cosmic time. The nakṣatra system, the tithi (lunar day), and the muhūrta (auspicious time) are all expressions of Kāla.

## Metallurgy

The concept of Kāla in metallurgy: the right time for metallurgical processes — certain times are more auspicious for smelting, forging, and casting. The concept of kāla-karma (time-action) in metallurgy.

## Ritual

The concept of Kāla in ritual: all Vedic rituals are performed at specific times determined by Jyotiṣa. The concept of muhūrta (auspicious time) — the right moment for ritual action. The concept of kāla-pūjā (worship of time) — the Kālī pūjā is the worship of the Goddess of time.

## Symbolism

The wheel (cakra) symbolizes Kāla — the wheel of time that turns without stopping. The serpent eating its own tail (Ouroboros) symbolizes the cyclical nature of time. The skull (kapāla) symbolizes Kāla as death. The hourglass symbolizes the finite nature of human time within infinite cosmic time.

# Chakras

## Canonical Name

Chakras

## Sanskrit

चक्राणि

## Transliteration

Cakrāṇi

## Śabda

चक्र (Cakra)

## Dhātu

क्रम् (Kram) / चक् (Cak) — To move, rotate, turn, shine.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from verbal root क्रम् / चक् with reduplication and suffix -ra. Neuter noun, plural form चक्राणि (Cakrāṇi). Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.1.114. Refers to subtle energy centers or vortices.

## Nirukta

Yāska's Nirukta: "cakram cakanaṁ vā, kramaṇam vā, krayam vā" — that which revolves or moves forward continuously. Chakras are psycho-spiritual centers of energy flow along the central channel (Suṣumnā nāḍī).

## Bīja

लँ, वँ, रँ, यँ, हँ, ॐ (Laṁ, Vaṁ, Raṁ, Yaṁ, Haṁ, Om) — the root seed syllables for the six major chakras plus Sahasrāra.

## Tattva

Cakra-Tattva — the subtle energy centers regulating the transformation of prāṇa and tattvas within the subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra).

## Śakti

Kuṇḍalinī-Śakti — the dormant spiritual evolutionary force coiled at Mūlādhāra chakra, which pierces the six chakras (Ṣaṭ-Cakra-Bheda) to unite with Śiva at Sahasrāra.

## Literal Meaning

Wheels, vortices, dynamic circles, energy hubs.

## Functional Meaning

Chakras are primary psycho-energetic nodes located along the central spinal axis where nāḍīs (energy channels) intersect. They govern physical organ systems, emotional patterns, mental states, and spiritual awakening stages. The primary seven chakras are Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddha, Ājñā, and Sahasrāra.

## Ontology

In Tantra and Hatha Yoga: Chakras are real energetic structures composed of subtle matter (sūkṣma-tattva). In Śāktism: They are divine lotus thrones (padma) of presiding deities and śaktis within the body.

## Cosmology

The seven chakras correspond macrocosmically to the seven upper lokas (Bhūḥ to Satyaloka) and the seven cosmic elements (Pañca-Mahābhūta + Manas + Buddhi).

## Psychology

Each chakra represents a psychological stage of human evolution: survival (Mūlādhāra), sexuality/creativity (Svādhiṣṭhāna), power/will (Maṇipūra), love/compassion (Anāhata), communication/truth (Viśuddha), intuition/wisdom (Ājñā), and divine unity (Sahasrāra).

## Governance

Chakra balances inform self-governance and leadership ethics (Rājadharma): leaders operating from heart (Anāhata) and wisdom (Ājñā) chakras govern with dharma and compassion.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda and Siddha medicine: Chakras correspond to major nerve plexuses (e.g., sacral, solar plexus, cardiac, carotid) and endocrine glands (thyroid, pituitary, pineal). Imbalances manifest as physical disease.

## Engineering

Bio-energetic architecture in Vāstu builds spaces aligning with the body's chakra axis, balancing thermal, magnetic, and acoustic resonances.

## Mathematics

Each chakra features a precise number of lotus petals (4, 6, 10, 12, 16, 2, 1000), total 50 petals corresponding to the 50 letters of the Sanskrit alphabet (Mātṛkā-varṇa).

## Astronomy

Chakra energies align with planetary presences: Saturn (Mūlādhāra), Jupiter (Svādhiṣṭhāna), Mars (Maṇipūra), Venus (Anāhata), Mercury (Viśuddha), Sun/Moon (Ājñā).

## Metallurgy

Rasashāstra links specific metallic ashes (bhasmas) to individual chakra activations (e.g., Suvarṇa bhasma with Sahasrāra, Loha bhasma with Maṇipūra).

## Ritual

Nyāsa (ritual placement of mantras and touch upon body locations) systematically activates and sanctifies the chakras prior to worship or meditation.

## Symbolism

Symbolized by multi-petaled lotuses containing geometric yantras, seed syllables, animal mounts, and presiding male-female deity pairs.

# Shakti

## Canonical Name

Shakti

## Sanskrit

शक्ति

## Transliteration

Śakti

## Śabda

शक्ति

## Dhātu

शक् (Śak) — To be able, to have power, to be capable.

## Vyākaraṇa

Śakti is a feminine noun, i-stem declension. Derived from the root śak (to be able) with the suffix -ti. The feminine gender is significant — power in the Indian tradition is inherently feminine.

## Nirukta

"Śaknoti iti śaktiḥ" — that which is capable, that which has power. Śakti is both the power itself and the Goddess who embodies that power.

## Bīja

ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the primary bīja of Śakti. Also क्रीं (Krīm) — the bīja of Kālī-Śakti; ऐं (Aim) — the bīja of Sarasvatī-Śakti; श्रीं (Śrīm) — the bīja of Lakṣmī-Śakti.

## Tattva

Śakti-Tattva — the principle of divine power and creative energy. In Śākta philosophy: Śakti is the ultimate reality — Brahman as dynamic power. In Śaiva philosophy: Śakti is Śiva's inseparable power — "Śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavitum" (Śiva united with Śakti is capable of creating — Soundaryalaharī 1).

## Śakti

Śakti is itself the principle of śakti — it is self-referential. The three primary śaktis: Icchā-Śakti (will-power), Jñāna-Śakti (knowledge-power), Kriyā-Śakti (action-power).

## Literal Meaning

Power; energy; capability; the Goddess; the divine feminine principle.

## Functional Meaning

Śakti is the dynamic, creative, and liberating power of the universe. It is the feminine principle that activates the masculine principle (Śiva/Puruṣa). Without Śakti, Śiva is śava (a corpse) — inert. Śakti manifests as the three primary powers: Icchā (will), Jñāna (knowledge), and Kriyā (action). In the individual, Śakti manifests as kuṇḍalinī — the dormant power at the base of the spine that, when awakened, leads to liberation.

## Ontology

In Śākta philosophy: Śakti is the ultimate reality — Brahman as dynamic power. The Goddess (Devī) is not a secondary deity but the supreme reality. In Kashmir Śaivism: Śakti is Śiva's inseparable power — the universe is Śiva-Śakti's dance. In Advaita: Śakti is Brahman's māyā-śakti — the creative power of the absolute. In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is the equivalent of Śakti — the primal creative power.

## Cosmology

In Śākta cosmology: the universe is the Goddess's body — she is both the creator and the creation. The Devī Māhātmya describes Śakti as the power that creates, preserves, and dissolves the universe. The concept of Śakti-pīṭhas (power seats) — 51 or 108 sacred sites where the Goddess's power is concentrated.

## Psychology

Śakti as psychological principle: the three śaktis (icchā, jñāna, kriyā) correspond to will, intellect, and action in the individual. Kuṇḍalinī-śakti is the psychological-spiritual power that, when awakened through yoga, transforms consciousness. The concept of śakti-pāta (descent of grace) — the Guru's transmission of śakti to the student.

## Governance

The concept of Śakti in governance: the ruler's power (rāja-śakti) is a manifestation of divine Śakti. The Arthaśāstra describes three types of royal power: prabhāva-śakti (power of majesty), mantra-śakti (power of counsel), utsāha-śakti (power of energy). The concept of rāṣṭra-śakti (national power) in Indian political philosophy.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Śakti is the vital power (ojas) — the refined essence of all bodily tissues. The concept of śakti in Āyurvedic therapy: building ojas (vital power) through proper diet, lifestyle, and herbs. The concept of śakti-vardhana (power enhancement) in Āyurvedic medicine.

## Mathematics

The concept of Śakti in mathematics: the power function (śakti) in Indian mathematics — the concept of raising a number to a power. The Bījaganita (algebra) of Bhāskara uses śakti in the sense of "square" (the power of a number).

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Śakti is associated with the Moon (Candra) and Venus (Śukra) — the feminine planets. The concept of graha-śakti (planetary power) — each planet has its own śakti. The nakṣatra Śakti is associated with specific astrological powers.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: Śakti is the feminine principle in alchemy — sulfur (gandhaka) is the Śakti to mercury's (pārada) Śiva. The union of mercury and sulfur is the alchemical Śiva-Śakti union. The concept of dhātu-śakti (power of metals) — each metal has its own śakti.

## Ritual

The Śakti-pūjā (worship of the Goddess) is the primary Śākta ritual. The Navārātra (nine nights of the Goddess) is the primary Śākta festival. The concept of śakti-upāsanā (worship of power) — using the Goddess's power for liberation. The Tantric ritual of śakti-sādhana (practice with the Goddess's power).

## Symbolism

The triangle (trikona) pointing downward symbolizes Śakti — the feminine, receptive, creative power. The lotus symbolizes Śakti's creative power — blooming from the waters of consciousness. The lion (siṃha) is Śakti's vehicle — representing her power over the ego. The trident (triśūla) represents Śakti's three powers (icchā, jñāna, kriyā).

# Prana

## Canonical Name

Prana

## Sanskrit

प्राण

## Transliteration

Prāṇa

## Śabda

प्राण

## Dhātu

प्र + अन् (Pra + An) — Pra (forward, forth) + An (to breathe, to live). That which breathes forth; the forward-moving breath.

## Vyākaraṇa

Prāṇa is a masculine noun. The prefix pra- (forward) combined with the root an- (to breathe) gives prāṇa — the primary, forward-moving life-breath. Distinguished from the five vāyus: Prāṇa (inward breath), Apāna (downward breath), Samāna (equalizing breath), Udāna (upward breath), Vyāna (pervading breath).

## Nirukta

"Prāṇiti iti prāṇaḥ" — that which breathes is prāṇa. The life-force that animates all living beings.

## Bīja

यं (Yaṃ) — the bīja of vāyu (air/wind), the element most closely associated with prāṇa. Also हं (Haṃ) — the bīja of the throat chakra (Viśuddha) associated with prāṇa's vocal expression.

## Tattva

Prāṇa-Tattva — the life-force principle. Prāṇa is the bridge between the physical body (annamaya kosha) and the mind (manomaya kosha). It is the animating principle that distinguishes the living from the dead.

## Śakti

Prāṇa-Śakti — the vital power. The śakti that animates all living beings. In Śākta traditions, prāṇa-śakti is the Goddess's life-giving power manifest in every breath.

## Literal Meaning

Breath; life-force; vital energy; the animating principle.

## Functional Meaning

Prāṇa is the universal life-force that animates all living beings. It operates through the prāṇamaya kosha (energy sheath) and the network of nāḍīs (energy channels). The five prāṇas (pañca-vāyu) govern specific physiological functions: Prāṇa (respiration, heart), Apāna (elimination, reproduction), Samāna (digestion, assimilation), Udāna (speech, upward movement, death), Vyāna (circulation, distribution). Prāṇāyāma (breath control) is the primary yogic practice for working with prāṇa.

## Ontology

In Vedic ontology: Prāṇa is the cosmic life-force — "prāṇo vai brahma" (Prāṇa is indeed Brahman — Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad). In Sāṃkhya: Prāṇa is the activity of the subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra). In Advaita: Prāṇa is the manifestation of Brahman as the life-force. In Āyurveda: Prāṇa is the primary vāta-doṣa — the governing principle of all movement and nervous function.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: Prāṇa is the cosmic breath — the universe breathes in and out through cosmic cycles (kalpa). The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad describes a cosmic debate among the prāṇas to determine which is supreme — prāṇa (breath) wins because when it leaves, all other faculties cease. In Purāṇic cosmology: Prāṇa is the breath of Brahma — the universe is created on his outbreath and dissolved on his inbreath.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology: prāṇa and mind (manas) are intimately connected — "prāṇe manaḥ" (the mind is in prāṇa). Controlling prāṇa through prāṇāyāma controls the mind. The concept of prāṇa-spanda (the vibration of prāṇa) in Kashmir Śaivism is the basis of all mental activity. The five prāṇas govern different psychological functions: Prāṇa (attention, perception), Apāna (letting go, release), Samāna (integration, balance), Udāna (aspiration, will), Vyāna (expansion, connection).

## Governance

The concept of prāṇa in governance: the king's prāṇa (vitality) is the prāṇa of the kingdom. The Arthaśāstra prescribes prāṇāyāma and yoga for the ruler's mental clarity. The concept of rāṣṭra-prāṇa (the life-force of the nation) appears in political philosophy.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Prāṇa is the primary vāta-doṣa governing the nervous system, respiration, and all movement. Prāṇa-vāyu specifically governs the heart and respiratory system. Prāṇa imbalance is the root of all vāta disorders. Prāṇāyāma is the primary Āyurvedic therapy for prāṇa disorders. The concept of prāṇa-pratīkāra (prāṇa therapy) includes breath work, marma therapy, and yoga.

## Mathematics

The concept of prāṇa in mathematics: the Vedic concept of prāṇa as the animating principle of numbers — each number has its own prāṇa (vitality). The concept of prāṇa in Vedic meter (chandas): each meter has a specific prāṇa (breath pattern) that gives it its power.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Prāṇa is associated with the Sun (Sūrya) — the cosmic prāṇa-source. The concept of prāṇa-āyuṣa (life-span calculation) in Jyotiṣa uses prāṇa as the unit of time. The prāṇa (a unit of time = 4 seconds) is the smallest unit in Vedic time measurement.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: prāṇa is the life-force that must be infused into alchemical preparations. The concept of prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā (installation of life-force) in idol-making is the ritual infusion of prāṇa into a metal image. Mercury (pārada) is considered the prāṇa of metals in Rasaśāstra.

## Ritual

Prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā (installation of life-force) is the ritual that animates a deity's image. The prāṇāyāma performed before ritual purifies the prāṇa of the practitioner. The concept of prāṇa-āhuti (offering of prāṇa) in yajña — the breath itself is offered to the fire.

## Symbolism

The breath symbolizes prāṇa — the most immediate experience of life-force. The wind (vāyu) symbolizes prāṇa's invisible, pervading nature. The serpent (nāga) symbolizes prāṇa's movement through the nāḍīs. The lotus symbolizes prāṇa's blooming in the heart.

# Akasha

## Canonical Name

Akasha

## Sanskrit

आकाश

## Transliteration

Ākāśa

## Śabda

आकाश

## Dhātu

आ + काश् (Ā + Kāś) — Ā (towards, completely) + Kāś (to shine, to be luminous). That which shines completely; the luminous space.

## Vyākaraṇa

Ākāśa is a masculine noun derived from the prefix ā- and the root kāś (to shine). The word conveys both the sense of "space" and "luminosity" — space is not empty but luminous.

## Nirukta

"Ākāśate iti ākāśaḥ" — that which shines. Space is not mere emptiness but the luminous ground of all existence.

## Bīja

हं (Haṃ) — the bīja of the space element (ākāśa) in Tantric traditions. Associated with the Viśuddha chakra (throat — the space center).

## Tattva

Ākāśa-Tattva — the space principle. The first and subtlest of the five mahābhūtas (great elements): Ākāśa (space), Vāyu (air), Agni (fire), Āp (water), Pṛthvī (earth). Ākāśa is the substratum of all other elements — they all exist within space.

## Śakti

Ākāśa-Śakti — the power of infinite space. The śakti that provides the ground for all manifestation. In Tantric traditions, ākāśa is the śakti of pure potentiality.

## Literal Meaning

Space; ether; sky; the luminous void.

## Functional Meaning

Ākāśa is the subtlest of the five elements — the space in which all other elements and all phenomena exist. It is the medium of sound (śabda) — sound travels through ākāśa. In Vedānta, ākāśa is the first element to emerge from Brahman in the process of creation. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad teaches that Brahman is ākāśa — the infinite space of consciousness.

## Ontology

In Vaiśeṣika: Ākāśa is one of the nine dravyas (substances) — it is eternal, all-pervading, and the substratum of sound. In Advaita: Ākāśa is the first manifestation of Brahman — "ākāśo ha vai nāma nāmarūpayor nirvahitā" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1). In Sāṃkhya: Ākāśa is the first tanmātra (subtle element) — śabda-tanmātra (sound-essence) — from which the gross space element emerges.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: Ākāśa is the first element created — from Brahman comes ākāśa, from ākāśa comes vāyu, from vāyu comes agni, from agni comes āp, from āp comes pṛthvī (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1). The concept of cidākāśa (consciousness-space) — the infinite space of pure awareness that is Brahman.

## Psychology

Ākāśa as psychological principle: the mind (manas) is like ākāśa — it provides the space in which thoughts arise and dissolve. The concept of cidākāśa (consciousness-space) — the pure awareness that is the ground of all mental activity. The practice of ākāśa-dhāraṇā (concentration on space) leads to the experience of infinite consciousness.

## Governance

The concept of ākāśa in governance: the ruler who governs from the space of ākāśa (non-attachment, equanimity) governs wisely. The concept of rāja-ākāśa (the space of the king) — the king's court as the space where all voices are heard.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Ākāśa is the element associated with the vāta doṣa (along with vāyu). The concept of ākāśa in the body: the spaces within the body (channels, cavities) are the body's ākāśa. Ākāśa imbalance leads to vāta disorders — anxiety, dryness, instability.

## Mathematics

The concept of ākāśa in mathematics: the concept of infinite space (ananta-ākāśa) is the philosophical basis for the Indian mathematical concept of infinity. The concept of śūnya (zero) as the mathematical ākāśa — the empty space from which all numbers emerge.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Ākāśa is the space in which all celestial bodies move. The concept of ākāśa-gaṅgā (the Milky Way — the river of space). The nakṣatra system maps the ākāśa into 27 divisions.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: ākāśa is the space in which alchemical transformations occur. The concept of ākāśa as the medium of subtle influences — the alchemist works with the ākāśa of the laboratory.

## Ritual

The concept of ākāśa in ritual: the ritual space (yajña-śālā) is a consecrated ākāśa — a space set apart from ordinary space. The concept of maṇḍala (sacred circle) as a bounded ākāśa. The concept of ākāśa-dīpa (sky lamp) — a lamp offered to the infinite space.

## Symbolism

The sky (ākāśa) symbolizes infinite space, freedom, and the divine. The blue color symbolizes ākāśa — the sky's color. The void (śūnya) symbolizes ākāśa's nature as the ground of all existence. The mirror symbolizes ākāśa — it reflects all without being affected.
